public.subject: Programming
public.title: Programming 1 (Python)
public.goal: Learn to program from the very start: work out exact steps on paper, then write them in Python. Values and names, decisions, loops, functions, collections, files and errors, each taught from first basics and practised on real tasks. By the end you can design, build, test and explain a small program that solves a real problem.

units.title: Solving before coding
units.focus: What a program is, algorithms on paper, flowcharts and pseudocode, your first Python, and reading error messages.

units.title: Values and names
units.focus: Variables, numbers, text, input and output, and types.

units.title: Decisions
units.focus: Turning rules into if, elif and else, combining conditions, testing the edges, and nested decisions.

units.title: Loops
units.focus: while and for, ranges, the common loop patterns, nested loops, tracing, and fixing loop bugs.

units.title: Functions
units.focus: Defining and calling functions, parameters and return values, scope, decomposition and testing.

units.title: Collections
units.focus: Lists, strings as sequences, dictionaries, sets, tuples, and choosing between them.

units.title: Files and errors
units.focus: Reading and writing files, CSV data, handling errors, modules, libraries, and a whole program start to finish.

project.title: A tool that solves a real problem of yours

blocks.text: Build a small Python tool that solves a real problem of your own. Good choices: a budget or transport tracker, a study-time log with weekly totals, a marks calculator that tells you what you need on the next test, or a tool that tidies and summarises a CSV file you really use. Keep it to something you can finish: about 60 to 200 lines.
Your project needs these six parts.

items: **The request.** One paragraph describing the problem in ordinary words, and a table of exact decisions: what goes in, what comes out, and what happens in the unclear cases, such as empty input or a bad value.
**The design.** A list of your functions, each with what it takes, what it returns and its one job. Working-out functions must return values, and only one place should read files or print.
**The tests.** At least eight `assert` tests written before or alongside the code, covering typical cases, edges, empty input and bad input.
**The program.** Working Python that reads real or realistic data from a file, handles bad rows by counting them, and writes or prints a clear result.
**The check.** One small input whose answer you worked out by hand, and the program's answer beside it.
**The report.** Half a page: what the tool does, how to run it, the decisions you made, what it doesn't do, and one thing you'd improve.

blocks.text: Write it yourself. Your own reasoning is the point, so don't have an AI write the code or the report. You may look things up in documentation. This project is self-checked, and the app will record it that way. Keep private details out of the data: no account numbers, passwords or other people's personal details.

rubric: All six parts are present, and the tool solves a real problem of mine.
Each function does one job, and the working-out functions return values.
I have at least eight tests, including edges, empty input and bad input, and they all pass.
I checked one answer by hand, and it matched.
I could explain any line of the program aloud.

lessons.title: What a program is
lessons.goal: Say what a program is, what source code and an interpreter are, why a computer needs instructions with no room for guessing, and what a bug is.
lessons.why: Programming is the core skill of a computing degree, and it starts with an idea, not a language. A program is a set of instructions so exact that a machine with no common sense can follow them. Once that idea is clear, every later lesson is about how to write those instructions in Python. It's also the habit that makes you useful at work: describing a process so precisely that nothing is left to guess.

blocks.text: A **program** is a sequence of instructions that tells a computer exactly what to do. The computer follows them literally, one after another, extremely fast, and without any understanding of what you meant.

Imagine giving directions to a friend: "Go to the market and get some tomatoes." Your friend fills in a hundred details: which market, how many, what to do if there are none. A computer fills in nothing. It needs to be told which market, how many, what to pay, and what to do if they're sold out.

head: Human instruction
What a computer needs
rows: Which marks, where they are stored, and where to put the total
The pass mark, which score to compare, and what to show either way
When "later" is, in minutes or as a date and time

blocks.text: This is the main skill of programming. Typing code is the easy part. Working out exactly what you mean, with every case covered, is the real work.
You write a program as **source code**: text in a programming language that people can read and write. Here's a whole program in Python:

blocks.code:
print("Welcome to 4YOS")
print(2 + 3)

blocks.text: As you learned in How Computers Work, a processor can only run machine code. So something has to turn your source code into actions. Python uses an **interpreter**: a program that reads your source code and carries it out, line by line. Other languages, such as C, use a **compiler**, which translates the whole program into machine code first, and then runs it.

head: Interpreter
Compiler
rows: Reads and runs the program, line by line
Translates the whole program first, then it runs
When the interpreter reaches the bad line
Usually before the program runs at all

blocks.text: You'll write Python in the boxes inside 4YOS lessons. The app has its own copy of the Python interpreter, so your code runs on your laptop, without the internet.

sections.title: Programs are made of a few kinds of step

blocks.text: Most programs, however large, are built from the same small set of actions:

head: Kind
What it does
Example
rows: Read what the user typed, or open a file
Print to the screen, or write a file
If the mark is 40 or more, say "pass"
For every student, print their mark

blocks.text: These match the input, processing and output you met before, with decisions and repetition giving the processing its power. You'll learn each of them in this course, one at a time.
A **bug** is a mistake in a program that makes it behave differently from what you intended. Every programmer writes bugs. The skill is finding and fixing them. There are three main kinds:

head: Kind
What happens
Example
rows: Python can't understand the code, so it won't run
It starts, then stops with an error
It runs, but gives the wrong answer

blocks.text: Syntax errors are the easiest to fix, because Python tells you where it got confused. Runtime errors come with a message too. Logic errors are the most dangerous, because nothing warns you. The program runs and confidently gives the wrong answer. That's why you'll always test your programs with cases where you already know the right answer.
Thinking the computer "knows what you meant". It never does. If your program gives a wrong answer, the instructions you wrote produce that answer. The fix is in your instructions.

warmup.question: What are the three stages every computer task goes through?
warmup.answer: Input, processing and output.

warmup.question: Why can't a processor run Python directly?
warmup.answer: A processor only runs machine code, so Python has to be translated or interpreted first.

blocks.text: Pick a small real task you do often, such as working out what you'll spend on transport this week.

items: Write it as instructions for someone with no common sense, numbered, with nothing left to guess.
Label each step as input, output, calculation, decision or repetition.
Give your instructions to a friend or family member, and ask them to follow them exactly as written, even when that seems silly. Note every place they got stuck or did something unexpected.
Rewrite those steps so that they're exact.

blocks.text: Write your final instructions and the places where the first version needed a guess.

rubric: My instructions leave nothing to guess, including what to do in unusual cases.
I labelled each step with its kind.
I tested them on a real person and fixed the steps where they got stuck.

exercises.question: Rewrite "check if I passed" as instructions a computer could follow.
exercises.answer: For example: take the mark. If the mark is 40 or more, show "passed". Otherwise, show "not passed". The pass mark here is an example. Use your course's real one.

exercises.question: A program that should calculate an average gives 150 for marks of 50, 60 and 40. What kind of bug is this?
exercises.answer: A logic error. It runs, but the answer is wrong, probably because it added the marks and forgot to divide by 3.

exercises.question: What is the difference between source code and machine code?
exercises.answer: Source code is text in a language people write, like Python. Machine code is the processor's own instructions, in binary.

summary: A program is a sequence of exact instructions, followed literally.
Source code is the text you write. The Python interpreter reads and runs it, line by line.
Programs are built from input, output, calculation, decision and repetition.
Bugs are syntax errors, runtime errors or logic errors.
Logic errors don't warn you, so always test with known answers.

further.title: The Python Tutorial, whetting your appetite

lessons.title: Write and test a procedure by hand
lessons.goal: Write an algorithm precise enough to follow without judgment, including decisions and loops, trace it by hand with a table, and find its failures by testing normal, boundary and missing cases.
lessons.why: Most beginners find programming hard, not because of the language, but because they have not worked out what the steps are. This skill comes first. It is the core of COS 102 at both schools, which often asks for algorithms, pseudocode and flowcharts on paper. It's also what you do in security, when you ask what a system does in a case nobody planned for, and what you do at work when you document a process.

blocks.text: An **algorithm** is a finite sequence of precise steps that solves a problem. "Precise" means that two different people, or a machine, would do the same thing with the same input. A good algorithm has:

items: **Inputs**: what it starts with.
**Outputs**: what it produces, including what to report if there is no answer.
**Definite steps**: no step needs a guess.
**An end**: it always stops.

blocks.text: Compare these instructions for finding a file:

head: Vague
Precise
rows: Open the folder. For each file in the list, check if its name contains the search word
If the name contains the word, write down its full path
When the list ends, report how many paths you wrote down. If none, report "not found"

blocks.text: The word "right" hides all the hard work. Whenever a step uses words like "the right one", "properly" or "if needed", you still have thinking to do.
Every algorithm, however large, is built from three structures. Almost all of programming is just these.

head: Structure
Meaning
Plain example
rows: If the water is boiling, add rice. Otherwise wait
While the rice is hard, cook for two more minutes

blocks.text: Exam papers often want this in **pseudocode**, structured English that isn't tied to one language. Here is finding the largest number in a list.

blocks.code:
INPUT a list of numbers
SET largest to the first number
FOR each number in the list
    IF number > largest THEN
        SET largest to number
    END IF
END FOR
OUTPUT largest

blocks.text: A **flowchart** draws the same logic. Ovals mark start and end, rectangles are actions, diamonds are decisions with yes and no branches, and parallelograms are input and output. Use your lecturer's conventions in an exam.

Forgetting that a loop has to change something. "While the rice is hard, wait" works because cooking changes the rice. But "while the file isn't found, look in the same place" never ends, because nothing changes.
A **trace table** has a column for each value that changes and a row for each step. It lets you run an algorithm like a computer, and see exactly where it goes wrong.
Worked example: trace the algorithm above
The output is 9, which is correct. Tracing takes a minute, and in that minute you can catch errors that would take much longer to find in running code.

blocks.question: Trace the same algorithm with -5, -2, -8. What does it output?
blocks.answer: It starts with largest = -5. Then -2 is larger, so largest = -2. -8 isn't larger. The output is -2, which is correct, and it would have failed if we had started largest at 0 instead of the first number.

blocks.text: A procedure that works once isn't finished. Test it with cases chosen to break it.

head: Kind of test
What to try
Why
rows: Values at the edge of a rule: first, last, exactly on a limit
Most mistakes are right at the edge
A list with no items, a folder with no files
What about a word where you expected a number?

blocks.text: Write down the **expected** result before you run the test. Otherwise you tend to accept whatever you get.
Worked example: a grading rule
Rule as first written: "Below 40 is F. 40 to 70 is a pass. Above 70 is A."

head: Test
Expected
What the rule gives
Finding
rows: Did you mean 70 to be an A? If the official bands make 70 an A, the rule is wrong
Scores can't be above 100, so it needs a check

blocks.text: One rule, five tests and three problems. Nothing here needed a computer. These are exactly the kinds of errors that cause real bugs and real security holes: an edge nobody tested, or an input nobody expected.
Your school's real grade bands come from its own handbook. This table is only an example of testing a rule.

Different correct algorithms can take very different amounts of work. To find a name in a sorted list of 1,000 names, you could check each from the start, which can take 1,000 checks. Or you could open the middle, discard the half it can't be in, and repeat. That takes about 10 checks, since each one halves what remains. This is **binary search**, shown in CS50's famous phone book demonstration. You'll study this in depth later. For now, the thing to notice is that the design of the steps matters as well as whether they work.

warmup.question: What is a program?
warmup.answer: A sequence of exact instructions that a computer follows literally.

warmup.question: Which kind of bug runs without warning but gives a wrong answer?
warmup.answer: A logic error.

blocks.text: Write a real procedure from your own life, on paper. A good choice is deciding what to study tonight, or finding a file for a course.

items: Write the inputs and outputs. Say what's reported if there's no answer.
Write the steps in pseudocode using at least one decision and one loop. Avoid vague words like "the right one".
Make a trace table and trace it with a normal input.
Test three more cases: a boundary, an empty case and a tie. Write the expected result before tracing each.
Fix anything that failed, and write what you changed.

blocks.text: If you can, ask someone to follow your steps exactly as written. Whatever they get stuck on is a step that isn't yet precise.

rubric: My steps need no guessing, and every path has an end.
I traced it with a table, and wrote expected results before testing.
I tested a boundary, an empty case and a tie, and fixed what I found.

exercises.question: Write pseudocode to count how many numbers in a list are above 50.
exercises.answer: SET count to 0. FOR each number: IF number > 50 THEN add 1 to count. After the loop, OUTPUT count.

exercises.question: Trace your answer with 60, 50, 70, 10. What should it output?
exercises.answer: 60 yes (count 1), 50 no, since it's not above 50, 70 yes (count 2), 10 no. Output 2. The value 50 is the boundary test.

exercises.question: What's wrong with this procedure? "Repeat: take a number from the pile. Until the pile is empty, add it to the total."
exercises.answer: It's ambiguous, and it fails on an empty pile by trying to take a number first. Better: "While the pile isn't empty: take a number and add it to the total."

exercises.question: A rule says "free delivery for orders over ₦10,000". Which three order values should you test?
exercises.answer: ₦9,999, ₦10,000 and ₦10,001. Exactly ₦10,000 is the case that reveals whether "over" was meant strictly.

summary: An algorithm has inputs, outputs, definite steps and an end.
Everything is built from sequence, selection and repetition.
A loop must change something, or it never ends.
A trace table runs an algorithm by hand, one step at a time.
Test normal, boundary, empty, duplicate and unexpected cases, and write what you expect first.

further.title: Harvard CS50x, Week 0 notes on algorithms and pseudocode

lessons.title: Flowcharts and pseudocode
lessons.goal: Draw a correct flowchart and write clear pseudocode for any algorithm, translate between the two, and check both by tracing.
lessons.why: Many first-year computing exams ask for an algorithm as a flowchart or in pseudocode, on paper, with no computer. Both are ways of showing the logic without the details of one language. They also force you to make every decision and loop visible, which is where most mistakes hide. Later, at work, flowcharts are how teams agree on a process before anyone builds it.

blocks.text: A **flowchart** draws an algorithm as shapes joined by arrows. The arrows show the order. These are the common shapes, though your lecturer may use slightly different conventions, so follow theirs in an exam.
Rules that keep a flowchart correct:

items: Exactly **one start**, and every path must reach an **end**.
A **decision has two exits**, labelled Yes and No (or True and False).
Every shape except the end has an arrow **leaving** it.
A **loop** is an arrow going back up to an earlier step, usually from a decision.

blocks.text: Worked example: pass or fail

blocks.code:
( START )
            |
     / INPUT mark /
            |
     < mark >= 40 ? >
       Yes /     \ No
          /       \
 / OUTPUT "Pass" /  / OUTPUT "Not yet" /
          \       /
           ( STOP )

blocks.text: The pass mark of 40 is an example. Use your own course's.

**Pseudocode** writes the same logic as structured English. It isn't a real language, so there's no single correct way to write it. But exams expect it to be clear and consistent, and these keywords are common:
Indent whatever is inside an IF or a loop. It shows clearly which steps belong to which structure.
Worked example: the average of marks

blocks.code:
INPUT n                      // how many marks
IF n = 0 THEN
    OUTPUT "No marks entered"
ELSE
    SET total TO 0
    FOR i FROM 1 TO n
        INPUT mark
        SET total TO total + mark
    END FOR
    OUTPUT total / n
END IF

blocks.text: Notice the check for `n = 0` at the start. Without it, the last line would divide by zero. A good algorithm handles the empty case on purpose.
Writing pseudocode that's really just vague English, such as "work out the average". Pseudocode must still be precise: each line is one clear action, decision or loop.
Each structure has a matching shape pattern, so translating is mechanical once you know them.

head: Pseudocode
Flowchart
rows: A diamond, two branches, which join again below
A diamond. Yes leads into the body, which loops back to the diamond. No leads on
Set i to 1, a diamond asking "i ≤ n?", the body, then add 1 to i and loop back

blocks.text: A FOR loop has no shape of its own in a flowchart. You draw it as its parts: start a counter, test it, do the body, step the counter.
A diagram can look neat and still be wrong. Check it the same way as any algorithm: with a trace table and chosen test cases.

head: Check
What to look for
rows: Follow each branch. Does it reach STOP?
Does something in the loop move it towards ending?
Trace the exact edge values, such as a mark of exactly 40
What if there are no items?

blocks.text: Worked example: tracing the average with n = 3
The answer is 50, which is correct. Now trace with n = 0: it outputs "No marks entered" and never divides. That's the empty case handled.

warmup.question: What are the three structures every algorithm is built from?
warmup.answer: Sequence, selection and repetition.

warmup.question: What is a trace table?
warmup.answer: A table with a column for each changing value and a row for each step, used to run an algorithm by hand.

blocks.text: Do this on paper.

items: Choose a small real algorithm: for example, working out whether you can afford a list of items with the money you have.
Write it in pseudocode, with at least one IF and one loop, and a check for the empty case.
Draw the same algorithm as a flowchart, using the correct shapes.
Trace it with a normal case, a boundary case and an empty case. Write the expected result before each trace.
Fix anything that failed, in both forms.

blocks.text: Write your pseudocode, describe your flowchart's shapes in order, and list your three tests with their results.

rubric: My pseudocode is precise, with one action per line and consistent indentation.
My flowchart uses the correct shapes, with one start, labelled decisions and every path ending.
I traced it with normal, boundary and empty cases.

exercises.question: Which flowchart shape would show "total = total + mark"?
exercises.answer: A rectangle, because it's a process.

exercises.question: Write pseudocode that outputs the larger of two numbers, a and b.
exercises.answer: INPUT a, b. IF a > b THEN OUTPUT a ELSE OUTPUT b END IF. (If they're equal, either is fine, but say so.)

exercises.question: How do you draw `WHILE total < 100 DO ... END WHILE` as a flowchart?
exercises.answer: A diamond asking "total < 100?". Yes goes to the body, which arrows back to the diamond. No goes on to the next step.

summary: Ovals for start and end, parallelograms for input and output, rectangles for actions, diamonds for decisions.
A decision has two labelled exits. A loop is an arrow going back up.
Pseudocode is precise structured English: INPUT, OUTPUT, SET, IF, FOR, WHILE.
Each pseudocode structure maps to a shape pattern.
Check designs by tracing, including boundary and empty cases.

lessons.title: Your first Python program
lessons.source: The Python Tutorial · An informal introduction
lessons.goal: Write and run your first Python programs: print text and numbers, use Python as a calculator, add comments, and understand what happens when you press Run.
lessons.why: Everything until now was done on paper. Now you'll see a computer follow your instructions. Seeing your own code run, and seeing exactly what it does when you change one character, is how programming becomes real. The habits from this lesson, such as running small pieces and checking the output against what you expected, are the ones professional programmers use every day.

blocks.text: The simplest program shows something on the screen. In Python, `print` does that. Whatever you put inside the brackets is shown.

blocks.code:
print("Hello, Ayo")
print("I study computing and statistics")
blocks.output:
Hello, Ayo
I study computing and statistics

blocks.text: Text in a program goes inside quotation marks. Python calls a piece of text a **string**. You can use double quotes `"like this"` or single quotes `'like this'`, as long as the opening and closing marks match.
Each `print` starts a new line. The lines run in order, from top to bottom: that's **sequence**, the first of the three structures.
Printing several things
You can print several items in one `print`, separated by commas. Python puts a space between them.

blocks.code:
print("Total:", 25)
print("Marks", 70, 85, 90)

blocks.text: Numbers don't need quotes. Python works out a calculation and prints the answer.

blocks.code:
print(7 + 5)
print(20 - 8)
print(6 * 4)
print(15 / 4)
print(2 ** 10)

blocks.text: Python follows the same order of operations you learned in Numbers and Algebra: brackets first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. So `2 + 3 * 4` is 14, and `(2 + 3) * 4` is 20.

Putting a calculation in quotes. `print("7 + 5")` prints the text `7 + 5`, not 12. Quotes make the text a string, shown exactly as written. Without quotes, Python works out the expression. A bare word without quotes is treated as a name, and must have been given a value first.
A **comment** is a note for people reading the code. Python ignores it. A comment starts with `#` and runs to the end of the line.

blocks.code:
# Work out this week's transport cost
print(5 * 800)   # 5 days at ₦800 a day

blocks.text: Good comments explain **why**, not what the code obviously does. "5 days at ₦800 a day" helps a reader. "Multiply 5 by 800" just repeats the code. The ₦800 here is an invented example.

When you press **Run** in a 4YOS lesson box, the Python interpreter in the app reads your code from the top, runs each line in turn, and shows what it prints. If a line has a mistake, Python stops there and shows an error message. You'll learn to read those in the next lesson.
A good working habit:

items: **Predict** what your code will print before you run it.
**Run** it.
**Compare** the output with your prediction.
If they differ, find out why before changing anything.

blocks.text: Changing code at random until it works teaches you nothing, and it often hides the real mistake. Predicting first turns every run into a small test.
Small steps
Write a line or two, run, check, then add more. If you write fifty lines and then run them, and something's wrong, you don't know where. With two new lines, it's one of those two.
Worked example: building up a calculation

Suppose you want the cost of data for a term. Don't write the whole thing at once. Start with the weekly cost, run it, and check it against your head: if a bundle costs ₦1,000 and you buy two a week, the weekly cost should be 2,000. Then add the next line, for 13 weeks, and run again. You expect 26,000. If the program says 2,013, you know the mistake is in the line you just added: you typed `+` instead of `*`. The prices here are invented examples.

This is the same predict, run and compare habit, used one line at a time. It's slower for the first minute and much faster overall, because mistakes are found the moment they appear, while the cause is still obvious.

warmup.question: What does the Python interpreter do?
warmup.answer: It reads your source code and carries it out, line by line.

warmup.question: Why must an algorithm's steps be precise?
warmup.answer: So that a computer, or another person, does exactly the same thing every time, with nothing to guess.

blocks.text: Use the box below. Before each run, write down what you predict it will print.

items: Change the first line so it prints a greeting with your own name.
Set `weekly` to a real weekly cost of yours, such as transport, using a calculation: days times the daily cost.
Set `term` to that weekly cost times `term_weeks`, the number of weeks in your term. Change `term_weeks` if your term is a different length.
Add a comment on each calculation saying what the numbers mean.
Press **Test my code** to check that `weekly` and `term` are worked out from each other correctly.

blocks.text: Write down your predictions, and any that were wrong and why.

rubric: I predicted each output before running, and noted where I was wrong.
My calculations use real numbers from my life, with comments explaining them.
My code passes the test.
practice.starter:
print("Hello")

# Your real numbers: days per week, and the cost per day
days = 5
cost_per_day = 800

term_weeks = 13

# Replace the 0s: work out the weekly cost, then the cost for the term
weekly = 0
term = 0

print("Weekly:", weekly)
print("Term:", term)

lessons.tests:
assert weekly == days * cost_per_day, "weekly should be days times cost_per_day"
assert term == weekly * term_weeks, "term should be weekly times term_weeks"

exercises.question: What does `print("5 * 3")` show? And `print(5 * 3)`?
exercises.answer: The first shows the text `5 * 3`. The second shows 15.

exercises.question: What does `print(10 - 2 * 3)` show?
exercises.answer: 4, because multiplication comes first.

exercises.question: Write one line that prints your name and how many courses you take, separated by a space.
exercises.answer: For example: `print("Ada", 12)`.

summary: `print(...)` shows text or the result of a calculation.
Text goes in quotes, and numbers and calculations don't.
Python follows the usual order of operations.
`#` starts a comment, which Python ignores. Comments should explain why.
Predict, run, compare. Add code in small steps.

lessons.title: Reading error messages
lessons.source: The Python Tutorial · Errors and exceptions
lessons.goal: Read a Python error message calmly: find the line, name the kind of error, understand what Python is telling you, and fix it.
lessons.why: Every programmer sees error messages all day. Beginners often panic or start changing things at random, while experienced programmers read the message, because it usually tells them exactly what's wrong and where. Learning to read errors early saves you hours. It's also the start of debugging, a skill that matters in every computing job, and in security too, where error messages can reveal how a system works.

blocks.text: When Python can't continue, it stops and prints an **error message**, also called a **traceback**. It looks alarming, but it's Python being helpful. It tells you three things:

items: **Where**: the file and line number.
**What kind**: the error's name, such as `NameError`.
**Why**: a short explanation after the name.

blocks.text: Here's a program with a mistake, and what Python says:

blocks.code:
mark = 70
print(marks)
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 2, in <module>
NameError: name 'marks' is not defined. Did you mean: 'mark'?

blocks.text: Read it from the bottom up. The last line is the most important. `NameError` means Python met a name it doesn't know. It even suggests what you probably meant: `mark`. The line above says it happened on line 2.
Reading only the top of the message, "Traceback (most recent call last)", and giving up. The useful part is at the bottom.

sections.title: Common errors and what they mean

head: Error
What it means
Typical cause
rows: Python can't read the code at all
Missing bracket or quote, or a misspelled keyword
A typo, or using a name before giving it a value
An operation got the wrong kind of value
A count that turned out to be 0
The spacing at the start of a line is wrong

blocks.text: TypeError

blocks.code: print("Marks: " + 70)
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

blocks.text: Python means: you used `+` to join text, but you gave it a whole number. "str" is text, and "int" is a whole number. You can fix it with a comma instead: `print("Marks:", 70)`. You'll learn other fixes in a later lesson.
ZeroDivisionError

blocks.code: print(150 / 0)
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

blocks.text: This is the empty-case problem from the paper lessons, now in real code.

sections.title: Syntax errors point near the mistake

blocks.text: A `SyntaxError` happens before anything runs, because Python can't understand the code. Its message points to where Python got confused, which is often just after the real mistake.

blocks.code:
print("Hello"
print("World")

blocks.text: The first line is missing its closing bracket. Python only realises something's wrong when it reaches the next line, so the error may point there. When a syntax error points to a line that looks fine, **look at the line before it** too.
Common causes:

items: A bracket or quote opened and never closed.
A word misspelled, such as `pritn`.
A colon missing where one is needed, which you'll meet with decisions and loops.
**Read the last line.** Note the error name and the explanation.
**Find the line number**, and look at that line, and the one before it for syntax errors.
**Say in your own words** what Python is complaining about.
**Fix one thing**, then run again.
**If it's a new error, that's progress.** Repeat.

blocks.text: Fix one error at a time. Python stops at the first error it meets, so the message is always about the first problem, and fixing it may reveal the next.
When there's no error, but the answer is wrong

That's a logic error, and Python can't help you. Use the tracing method from the paper lessons: work out by hand what each line should produce, and compare. Printing values partway through is the code version of a trace table:

blocks.code:
total = 50 + 70
print("after adding:", total)
average = total / 2
print("average:", average)

warmup.question: What are the three kinds of bug?
warmup.answer: Syntax errors, runtime errors and logic errors.

warmup.question: What does `print(2 + 3 * 4)` show?

blocks.text: The program in the box has four separate errors. Fix them one at a time.

items: Press Run. Read the last line of the error, and write down its name and line.
Fix only that error, then run again.
Repeat until it runs, writing down each error name as you go.
Check the output is right: it should show the total and the average of the three marks.
Press **Test my code**.

blocks.text: Write the four error names in the order you met them, and the fix for each.

rubric: I read the last line of each error before changing anything.
I fixed one error at a time, and recorded each one.
My final code passes the test, and I checked its answer by hand.
practice.starter:
mark1 = 60
mark2 = 75
mark3 = 90

total = mark1 + mark2 + mrak3
print("Total:" , total

average = total / count
count = 3
print("Average: " + average)

lessons.tests:
assert total == 225, "total should be 225"
assert average == 75.0, "average should be 75.0"

exercises.question: What does `NameError: name 'totl' is not defined` most likely mean?
exercises.answer: A typo. The name was probably meant to be `total`.

exercises.question: Python reports a SyntaxError on line 5, and line 5 looks correct. Where else should you look?
exercises.answer: At line 4 and earlier, for a bracket or quote that was never closed.

exercises.question: `print("Age: " + 21)` gives a TypeError. What's one fix?
exercises.answer: Use a comma, `print("Age:", 21)`, so Python prints them as two items.

summary: An error message tells you where, what kind and why. Read it from the bottom up.
NameError is usually a typo, TypeError mixes kinds of value, ZeroDivisionError divides by zero.
For a SyntaxError, check the line shown and the line before it.
Fix one error at a time. A new error means progress.
No error but a wrong answer is a logic error: trace or print the values.

lessons.title: Values, names and expressions
lessons.goal: Store values under names, update them, build expressions from them, and predict exactly what a short program holds at each line.
lessons.why: A program that only prints fixed numbers can't do much. Variables let a program remember values, work with them, and change them as it goes, which is how every real program keeps track of a total, a score or a balance. Tracing what each variable holds, line by line, is the single most useful skill for understanding and fixing code.

blocks.text: A **value** is a piece of data: a number such as `70`, a decimal such as `3.75`, or text such as `"Ada"`. You've already printed values. On its own, though, a value disappears as soon as the line finishes. To use it again, you need to give it a name.
A **variable** is a name that refers to a value. You create one with an **assignment**: a name, an equals sign, and a value.

blocks.code:
mark = 70
name = "Ada"
print(name, mark)

blocks.text: Read `mark = 70` as "**mark gets 70**", not "mark equals 70". The `=` sign in Python doesn't state that two things are equal, as it does in maths. It's an instruction: work out the right side, then store it under the name on the left.
Changing a variable
A variable can be given a new value. The old one is replaced.

blocks.code:
balance = 5000
balance = balance - 1200
print(balance)

blocks.text: The second line looks impossible as maths, but as an instruction it's clear. Work out the right side first, `5000 - 1200`, which is 3800. Then store that as the new `balance`.
Reading `=` as "equals". `x = x + 1` isn't a false equation. It means "take the current x, add 1, and store the result back in x".

An **expression** is anything Python can work out to a single value: `70`, `mark + 5`, `(a + b) / 2`. You can use variables inside expressions, and Python uses whatever value each one holds at that moment.

blocks.code:
mark1 = 60
mark2 = 80
average = (mark1 + mark2) / 2
print(average)

blocks.text: A variable holds a value, not a formula
Python works out an expression once, when the line runs. Changing a variable later doesn't update anything worked out earlier.

blocks.code:
price = 500
total = price * 3
price = 800
print(total)

blocks.text: `total` was calculated as 1500 when `price` was 500. Changing `price` afterwards doesn't change `total`. This surprises people who've used spreadsheets, where a formula recalculates by itself.
To understand a program, trace what each variable holds after each line, just like a trace table on paper.

blocks.code:
count = 0
count = count + 1
count = count + 1
total = count * 10

blocks.text: If a program gives the wrong answer, tracing like this almost always shows where.

Tracing feels slow at first, but it gets quicker with practice, and it's how experienced programmers read unfamiliar code. When you meet a program you didn't write, don't try to understand it all at once. Go line by line, keeping a note of what each variable holds, exactly as the computer does. You'll often spot a mistake the moment a value in your table differs from what you expected. In exams, questions that ask "what does this program print?" are testing exactly this skill, and a neat trace table is the surest way to get them right.
Variable names must follow Python's rules:

items: Letters, digits and underscores only: `total_marks`, `mark2`.
They can't start with a digit: `2mark` is an error.
No spaces: `total marks` is an error.
Upper and lower case are different: `Mark` and `mark` are two different variables.
Some words are reserved by Python, such as `if`, `for` and `print`'s friends like `True`. Don't use them as names.

blocks.text: Good names say what the value means. `weekly_cost` is clear. `x` or `wc` makes the reader guess. Python programmers usually write names in lower case, with underscores between words.

warmup.question: What does `print(6 * 4)` show?
What does `NameError` usually mean?
warmup.answer: A misspelled name, or a name used before it was given a value.

exercises.question: After `a = 5`, then `a = a * 2`, then `a = a + 1`, what's in `a`?
exercises.answer: 11. It goes 5, then 10, then 11.

exercises.question: After `x = 4`, then `y = x + 1`, then `x = 10`, what's in `y`?
exercises.answer: 5. `y` was worked out when `x` was 4. Changing `x` later doesn't change `y`.

exercises.answer: `mark_2` and `Mark` are allowed. `2nd_mark` starts with a digit, and `my mark` has a space.

summary: A variable is a name that refers to a value.
`=` means "gets": work out the right side, then store it under the name.
An expression works out to one value, using what each variable holds right then.
Changing a variable later doesn't update values worked out earlier.
Names: letters, digits and underscores, not starting with a digit, case matters.

lessons.title: Numbers and arithmetic
lessons.goal: Use whole numbers and decimals in Python, divide in three different ways, use the remainder operator, round results for display, and know why decimals in a computer can be slightly off.
lessons.why: Most programs calculate something: marks, money, times, sizes. Python has two kinds of number and three kinds of division, and choosing the wrong one gives quietly wrong answers. The remainder operator is surprisingly useful, from telling even numbers from odd to converting minutes into hours. And knowing that decimals can be slightly inexact will save you from a classic bug in money and statistics code.

blocks.text: Python has two main kinds of number:
Python decides which kind from how you write it: `7` is an int, and `7.0` is a float. You can check with `type`:

blocks.code:
print(type(7))
print(type(7.0))

blocks.text: When you mix the two in a calculation, the result is a float: `3 + 0.5` is `3.5`.

Why have two kinds at all? Because they suit different jobs. A count of students is always whole, and an int stores it exactly. A measurement or an average often isn't whole, and a float can hold the decimal part. Choose by what the number means: a number of items is an int, and an amount that can be split, such as a height in metres, is a float.

`/` always gives a float, which may be very slightly approximate, even when it divides exactly: `10 / 2` is `5.0`. `//` floors the result, rounding down towards minus infinity, so `-7 // 2` is `-4`. `%` gives what's left over. Together, `//` and `%` are the long division you learned by hand: 17 divided by 5 is 3, remainder 2.

blocks.code:
print(10 / 2)
print(17 // 5)
print(17 % 5)

blocks.text: Uses of `//` and `%`
These come up constantly.

blocks.code:
minutes = 135
print(minutes // 60, "hours and", minutes % 60, "minutes")
print(14 % 2)
print(15 % 2)

blocks.text: A number is **even** if `n % 2` is 0, and odd if it's 1. Turning 135 minutes into hours and minutes uses `//` for the hours and `%` for the minutes left over.
Using `//` with negative numbers and expecting it to cut off the decimal. It rounds **down**: `-7 // 2` is `-4`, not `-3`. For counts and lengths, which are rarely negative, this seldom matters.
A calculation often gives more decimal places than you want to show. `round(value, places)` rounds to that many places:

blocks.code:
average = 200 / 3
print(average)
print(round(average, 2))

blocks.text: Python's `round` uses a rule called banker's rounding for numbers exactly halfway: it rounds them to the nearest even number, so `round(2.5)` gives 2 and `round(3.5)` gives 4. This avoids a small upward bias when you round many values. It rarely matters in practice, but it explains a result that otherwise looks wrong.
Round only when you **show** a result. Keep the full value for further calculations, exactly as with a calculator, or small rounding errors build up.
Computers store floats in binary, and many decimals, such as 0.1, can't be stored exactly in binary, just as 1/3 can't be written exactly in decimals. The difference is tiny, but it can show up:
This isn't a bug in Python. Every language that uses standard floats behaves this way. Two habits deal with it:

items: **Round for display**: `round(0.1 + 0.2, 2)` shows `0.3`.
**Count money in the smallest unit**: store amounts as whole kobo, using ints, so ₦12.50 is `1250`. Ints are always exact.

blocks.text: For most work, such as averages of marks or sizes of files, the tiny float error never matters, as long as you round what you show. It matters when you compare floats for exact equality, and when you add up many money amounts, where tiny errors can add up to a kobo or more. In those cases, use the two habits above.
Large numbers

Python ints can be as large as you like, so `2 ** 100` is worked out exactly. You can write large numbers with underscores to make them readable: `1_000_000` is one million. Python ignores the underscores.

summary: `int` is a whole number, and `float` is a decimal. Mixing them gives a float.
`/` gives a float. `//` floors, rounding down. `%` gives the remainder.
`n % 2` is 0 for even numbers.
Round with `round(value, places)` for display only.
Floats can be very slightly off. Round for display, and count money in whole kobo.

lessons.title: Text and strings
lessons.goal: Work with text in Python: join strings, build messages with f-strings, change case, tidy spaces, measure length and handle quotes inside text.
lessons.why: Most of what programs show people is text: names, messages, reports. A great deal of real data is text too: names in a register, lines in a log file, words in a password. Handling text well is a skill you'll use in every course, from writing a clear report in statistics to examining log files in security.

blocks.text: A **string** is a piece of text: letters, digits, spaces and symbols, inside quotes. `"Ada"`, `'COS 102'` and `"123"` are all strings. The last one looks like a number, but in quotes it's text, and Python treats it as text.
Joining strings
`+` joins two strings into one. This is called **concatenation**.

blocks.code:
first = "Ada"
last = "Okafor"
full = first + " " + last
print(full)

blocks.text: Notice the `" "` in the middle. Python only joins exactly what you give it, so without it you'd get `AdaOkafor`.
You can repeat a string with `*`: `"-" * 10` gives `----------`. That's handy for drawing lines in a report.
Joining a string and a number with `+`. `"Age: " + 21` is a TypeError. Use an f-string instead, explained next.
The clearest way to build a message from text and values is an **f-string**. Put `f` before the opening quote, and write any variable or expression inside curly brackets.

blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
mark = 78
print(f"{name} scored {mark} out of 100")
print(f"That's {mark / 100 * 100:.0f} percent, or {100 - mark} below full marks")
blocks.output:
Ada scored 78 out of 100
That's 78 percent, or 22 below full marks

blocks.text: Inside the brackets, Python works out the expression and puts its value into the text. f-strings work with numbers too, so you don't need to convert anything.

f-strings are the modern way to build text in Python, and you'll see them in most code written today. They're easier to read than joining many pieces with `+`, because the message reads in one piece, just as it will appear. Use them whenever a message mixes fixed words with values that change.
Formatting numbers
After a colon inside the brackets, you can control how a number appears:

head: Code
Shows
Meaning
rows: As a percentage, one decimal place

blocks.code:
price = 1500000
share = 0.256
print(f"₦{price:,}")
print(f"{share:.1%}")

blocks.text: A **method** is an action that belongs to a value. You write the value, a dot, then the method's name and brackets. Strings have many.

blocks.code:
typed = "  Okafor  "
clean = typed.strip().upper()
print(f"[{clean}]")

blocks.text: Methods don't change the original string. They give you a **new** one. `typed` still holds `"  Okafor  "` with its spaces. To keep the result, store it, as `clean` does here.
Methods can be chained: `typed.strip().upper()` strips first, then turns the result into capitals.

Tidying text like this matters more than it looks. Data typed by people is messy: extra spaces, random capitals, different spellings of the same thing. A program that compares "Ada" with " ada" finds them different, even though a person would say they're the same. Cleaning text before you compare, sort or store it is one of the most common jobs in real programs, from school registers to security logs. Strings have many more methods than the ones in the table, and the Python documentation lists them all.
`len` gives the number of characters in a string, including spaces:

blocks.code:
print(len("Ada"))
print(len("Ada Okafor"))

blocks.text: Quotes and new lines inside a string
If your text contains a quote, use the other kind outside: `"It's done"` or `'She said "yes"'`. A backslash begins an **escape sequence**, a code for something you can't type directly:

head: Escape
Means
rows: A double quote inside double quotes

blocks.code: print("Line one\nLine two")

warmup.question: What does `print("Marks: " + 70)` cause, and why?
warmup.answer: A TypeError, because `+` can't join text and a whole number.

warmup.question: After `a = 5`, then `b = a + 2`, what's in `b`?

Set `full` to the two clean parts joined with one space.
Set `message` to an f-string such as `"Welcome, Ada Okafor (10 characters)"`, using `len`.

exercises.question: What does `"ab" + "cd" + "ab"` give?
exercises.answer: `"abcdab"`.

summary: A string is text in quotes. `"123"` is text, not a number.
`+` joins strings. Add spaces yourself.
f-strings put values into text: `f"{name} scored {mark}"`.
Methods such as `.strip()` and `.upper()` return a new string. Store it to keep it.
`len` counts the characters, and `\n` makes a new line.

lessons.title: Input and output
lessons.source: The Python Tutorial · Input and output
lessons.goal: Get text from the person using your program with `input`, know that it always arrives as text, and control exactly how `print` shows results.
lessons.why: A program that always uses the same numbers can only ever give one answer. Input lets the same program answer a new question each time it runs: your marks this term, your budget this month. Almost every useful program takes input of some kind, from what a user types to what's in a file. And the most common beginner bug in Python, adding together two typed numbers and getting them joined as text, comes from this lesson.

blocks.text: `input` shows a message, called a **prompt**, waits for the person to type something and press Enter, and gives you what they typed.

blocks.code:
name = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Hello, {name}")

blocks.text: When this runs, the screen shows `What is your name? `, the person types `Ada` and presses Enter, and the program prints `Hello, Ada`. End the prompt with a space, so the typed answer doesn't touch the question.

The Python boxes in 4YOS lessons can't pause for you to type, so `input` examples here are shown as text, not run. In the practice boxes, we put what the person would have typed into a variable instead. In a full Python program on a computer, `input` works as described.
This is the key fact of this lesson. **Whatever the person types, `input` gives you a string**, even if they type a number. If they type `25`, you get `"25"`, the text, not the number 25.
That causes a classic bug:

blocks.code:
first = "20"    # what input would give if the person typed 20
second = "30"   # and 30
print(first + second)

blocks.text: `+` joins the two strings instead of adding the numbers. To do arithmetic, you must turn the text into a number first, with `int` for whole numbers or `float` for decimals:

blocks.code:
first = "20"
second = "30"
print(int(first) + int(second))

blocks.text: So the usual pattern for reading a number is:

blocks.code:
age = int(input("How old are you? "))
price = float(input("Price in naira: "))

blocks.text: You'll learn more about converting between types, and what happens when the text isn't a number, in the next lesson.

Forgetting the conversion. Your program runs with no error, and gives `2030` instead of `50`. It's a logic error, so nothing warns you. When a program reads numbers, convert them straight away, on the same line as `input`.
`print` has two useful options, written inside its brackets after the values.

head: Option
Default
What it changes
Example
rows: What comes after the last item
`print("a", end="")` doesn't start a new line

blocks.code:
print("2026", "11", "06", sep="-")
print("Loading", end="")
print("...done")

sections.title: A program that talks to people

blocks.text: A good interactive program does three things. It asks clearly, it checks what it got, and it answers in a way the person understands.

items: **Ask clearly**: say what you want and in what form. "Amount in naira, numbers only: " is better than "Enter: ".
**Tidy the input**: people add spaces and use odd capitals. Use `.strip()` and `.lower()` before using text answers.
**Answer clearly**: use an f-string with units, such as `f"You have ₦{left:,} left"`, not just a bare number.

blocks.text: Worked example: a budget check

blocks.code:
money = float(input("How much do you have, in naira? "))
cost = float(input("How much does it cost, in naira? "))
left = money - cost
print(f"After buying it, you'd have ₦{left:,.2f} left.")

blocks.text: Notice that both inputs are converted to `float` straight away, and the answer is formatted with commas and two decimal places. If the person types `5000` and `1250.50`, the program prints `After buying it, you'd have ₦3,749.50 left.`
Reading the program from top to bottom, you can see the input, processing and output stages you met in How Computers Work: two inputs, one calculation, one output.
What if they type `five thousand`? `float` can't convert that, and the program stops with an error. You'll learn to handle that politely in the Files and errors unit.

exercises.answer: The text `"7"`, a string.

summary: `input("prompt ")` waits for typing, and returns what was typed.
Input is always a string, even when the person types a number.
Convert straight away: `int(input(...))` or `float(input(...))`.
`sep` sets what goes between printed items, and `end` what comes after.
Ask clearly, tidy text input, and answer with units.

further.title: The Python Tutorial, input and output

lessons.title: Types and conversion
lessons.goal: Say what type any value has, convert between strings, ints, floats and booleans, and know what happens when a conversion can't work.
lessons.why: Every value in Python has a type, and the type decides what you can do with it. Adding two ints gives a sum. Adding two strings joins them. Most confusing bugs in beginners' programs come from a value having a different type from the one you thought. This lesson gives you the tools to check a type, change it on purpose, and recognise the errors when something can't be converted.

blocks.text: You've met three types. Here's the fourth, and a summary of all of them.

head: Type
Python name
Examples
Meaning
rows: Answers to yes or no questions

blocks.text: `""` is the **empty string**: text with nothing in it. It's still a string.
A **bool** (short for Boolean, after the mathematician George Boole) has only two values, `True` and `False`, with capital letters. Comparisons give bools:

blocks.code:
print(70 >= 40)
print("Ada" == "ada")
print(type(70 >= 40))

blocks.text: Bools are what decisions run on, as you'll see in the next unit.

Why does the type matter so much? Because the same symbol can mean different things for different types. For ints and floats, `+` adds. For strings, it joins. For a string and an int together, it fails. Python looks at the types of the values on each side and decides what to do. So when an operation surprises you, the first question to ask is: what types are these values, really? Very often, one of them is a string that only looks like a number.
Checking a type
`type` tells you what type a value has. When a program behaves strangely, printing the type of a value is often the quickest way to find out why.

blocks.code:
mark = "70"
print(type(mark))

blocks.text: Each type has a function with its name that converts other values into it.
Notice `int(3.99)` gives `3`. Converting a float to an int cuts off the decimal part. It doesn't round. If you want rounding, use `round(3.99)`, which gives `4`.
`str` is useful for joining numbers into text with `+`, though an f-string is usually clearer:

blocks.code:
port = 443
print("Port " + str(port))
print(f"Port {port}")

blocks.text: Expecting `int("3.5")` to work. `int` can turn `"3"` into 3, and `3.5` into 3, but not the text `"3.5"`. Use `float("3.5")` first, and then `int` if you really want a whole number.
If the text isn't a valid number, conversion fails with a `ValueError`:

blocks.code: print(int("twenty"))
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'twenty'

blocks.text: The message says that `'twenty'` isn't a whole number written in ordinary base ten digits. A `ValueError` means the type was right, a string, but the value couldn't be used. That's different from a `TypeError`, where the type itself was wrong.

head: Error
Meaning
Example
rows: The wrong type for this operation
The right type, but an unusable value

blocks.text: This distinction helps you fix problems faster. A TypeError tells you to look at what kind of value you have, and perhaps convert it. A ValueError tells you the kind is right, but the content is wrong, so look at exactly what was typed or read from the file.
Spaces at the ends are allowed, as `int(" 25 ")` gives 25. But a comma isn't: `int("1,500")` is a ValueError. Real typed numbers often contain commas, so tidy them first with `.replace(",", "")`.
`bool` converts values into `True` or `False`. The rule is simple: **empty or zero is False, and almost everything else is True**.
That last row catches people: `bool("False")` is `True`, because the string isn't empty. To turn typed yes or no answers into a bool, compare the text instead: `answer.strip().lower() == "yes"`.

warmup.question: What type does `input` always return?
warmup.answer: A string.

warmup.question: What's the difference between `7` and `7.0` in Python?
warmup.answer: `7` is an int, and `7.0` is a float.

`type(value)` tells you a value's type.
Convert with `int`, `float`, `str` and `bool`. `int(3.99)` cuts off to 3.
A ValueError means the right type but an unusable value, such as `int("twenty")`.
Empty or zero is False. Any non-empty string, even `"False"`, is True.

further.title: The Python Tutorial, input and output

lessons.title: Turn a rule into a decision
lessons.goal: Turn a rule written in words into an `if`, `elif` and `else` decision in Python, put the branches in the right order, and trace which branch runs for any value.
lessons.why: Decisions are what make programs useful. Without them, a program does the same thing every time. With them, it can tell a pass from a fail, a valid password from a weak one, or a cheap delivery from a free one. This is selection, the second of the three structures, now in real code. Writing the decision is easy. Getting its order and conditions exactly right is the skill, and the place where most real bugs hide.

blocks.text: A decision needs a question with a yes or no answer. In Python, you ask it with a **comparison**, which gives a bool: `True` or `False`.
Comparisons work on strings too. `"ada" == "ada"` is True, while `"Ada" == "ada"` is False, because case matters.
Using `=` to compare. `=` stores a value, and `==` compares. Writing `if mark = 40:` is a SyntaxError.
An `if` statement runs a block of code only when its condition is True.

blocks.code:
mark = 72
if mark >= 40:
    print("Passed")
print("Done")

blocks.text: Two details matter here. The `if` line ends with a **colon**. And the lines that belong to the `if` are **indented**, usually by four spaces. Indentation isn't decoration in Python: it's how Python knows which lines are inside the decision. `print("Done")` isn't indented, so it runs whatever the mark.
else
`else` gives a block to run when the condition is False:
elif
When there are more than two outcomes, add `elif`, short for "else if". Python checks each condition from the top, runs the **first** block whose condition is True, and skips all the rest.
These grade bands are an example. Your school's real bands come from its own handbook.

Trace it for a mark of 64. Is 64 at least 70? No, so Python skips that block. Is it at least 60? Yes, so `grade` becomes "B", and Python skips every remaining branch, including the `else`. Notice that the second condition doesn't need to say "and less than 70": by the time Python reaches it, it already knows the mark wasn't 70 or more, or the first branch would have run. That's why a well-ordered chain stays short and readable.
You can have as many `elif` branches as you need, and the `else` is optional. Without an `else`, if no condition is True, nothing in the chain runs at all, and the program carries on after it.
Because Python stops at the first True condition, the order of the branches can change the answer. Compare these two:

In the second version, any mark of 70 or more is also 40 or more, so the first branch catches it, and the `elif` never runs. When ranges overlap like this, **check the most specific or highest one first**.
Writing separate `if` statements when you meant one chain. Each separate `if` is checked on its own, so more than one can run. Use `elif` when only one outcome should happen.
A reliable way to turn a written rule into a decision:

items: **List every outcome** the rule can have.
**Write the condition** for each, using exact comparisons.
**Order them** so that no branch hides another.
**Decide the else**: what happens if nothing else matched?
**Trace** some values through it before running.

The rule: "Delivery is free for orders of ₦10,000 or more. Orders of ₦5,000 or more pay ₦500. Smaller orders pay ₦1,000." The prices are invented.

`if` runs its indented block when the condition is True. Don't forget the colon.
`elif` adds more outcomes. Python runs only the first True branch.
Put the highest or most specific condition first when ranges overlap.

lessons.title: Combining conditions
lessons.goal: Combine conditions with `and`, `or` and `not`, write ranges neatly, use `in` to check for one of several values, and avoid the classic mistakes when combining conditions.
lessons.why: Real rules rarely depend on one thing. "You can register if you've paid and you're not suspended." "The session ends if time is up or the user logs out." Combining conditions lets one decision express rules like these. It's also where some of the most common and most dangerous bugs live, especially in security checks, where one wrong `or` can let everyone in.

blocks.text: Three words combine bools into one answer.

head: Operator
True when
Example
Result
rows: At least one side is True

blocks.text: This table shows every combination:
This is the same logic you met with logic gates in How Computers Work, where AND, OR and NOT are built in hardware.

blocks.code:
paid = True
suspended = False
if paid and not suspended:
    print("You can register")

blocks.text: Worked example: tracing a combined condition

Take the rule "free entry for students, or for anyone under 12", with `student = False` and `age = 9`. The condition is `student or age < 12`. Work it out piece by piece, as Python does. `student` is False. `age < 12` is `9 < 12`, which is True. `False or True` is True, so entry is free. Now try `student = False` and `age = 30`: `False or False` is False, so they pay.

Python also takes a shortcut called **short-circuiting**. For `or`, if the left side is already True, the answer must be True, so Python doesn't even look at the right side. For `and`, if the left side is False, the answer must be False. This matters later, when the right side does something that could fail, such as dividing: `count > 0 and total / count > 50` never divides by zero, because when `count` is 0, Python stops at the left side.
Order of evaluation

`not` is worked out first, then `and`, then `or`. So `a or b and c` means `a or (b and c)`. When you combine `and` with `or`, add brackets to make your meaning clear, even when they aren't strictly needed.
To check that a value is between two limits, you can join two comparisons with `and`:
Python also lets you write the range the way it's written in maths. `60 <= mark < 70` means exactly the same thing, and reads more clearly:

blocks.code:
mark = 64
print(60 <= mark < 70)

sections.title: Checking for one of several values

blocks.text: To check whether a value is one of a list of options, `or` gets long:

blocks.code: if day == "Saturday" or day == "Sunday":

blocks.text: `in` is shorter and clearer. It checks whether the value appears among the ones in brackets:
`in` also checks whether one string appears inside another: `"@" in email` is True if the email contains an @.
This looks right, and it's wrong:

It printed "Warm colour" for green! Python reads it as `(colour == "red") or ("blue")`. The first part is False. The second part is just the string `"blue"`, and a non-empty string counts as True. So the whole condition is always True.
Each side of `or` must be a full comparison: `colour == "red" or colour == "blue"`. Or, better: `colour in ("red", "blue")`.
`if x == 1 or 2:` always passes. When the comparison is False, `or` gives 2, and `if` treats a nonzero 2 as true. Write `x == 1 or x == 2`, or `x in (1, 2)`.
Truthiness in conditions

You learned that empty and zero values count as False, and others as True. An `if` uses that directly. `if name:` runs when `name` isn't empty. It's a short way to check that something was typed, but be careful with numbers: `if count:` is False when the count is 0, even though 0 can be a real, correct count.

warmup.question: In an if, elif and else chain, how many branches run?
warmup.answer: Exactly one: the first whose condition is True, or else.

warmup.answer: False, because case matters.

`not` is worked out first, then `and`, then `or`. Use brackets to be clear.
Ranges can be written as `60 <= mark < 70`.
`x in (a, b, c)` checks for one of several values.

lessons.title: Testing the edges
lessons.goal: Find the values where a decision changes its answer, test exactly on and around them, catch off-by-one mistakes, and decide what your code should do with input outside the rule.
lessons.why: Most decisions work for typical values and fail at the edges: exactly on a limit, just past it, or with something nobody expected. Those failures are real bugs, and in security they're often real attacks, because attackers deliberately try the edges. Testing the edges takes a few minutes, and it catches the mistakes that ordinary testing misses.

blocks.text: Every comparison has an edge: a value where its answer flips from True to False. For `mark >= 40`, the edge is at 40: 39 gives False, and 40 gives True. A decision with several branches has an edge for each one.

Bugs cluster at edges because words in rules are slippery. Does "over 40" include 40? Does "up to 5 days" include day 5? The person who wrote the rule may not have decided, and the person who wrote the code may have guessed differently.
When a rule is unclear, don't guess: find out what was meant, and write it down.

sections.title: Test on and around every edge

blocks.text: For each edge, test three values: **just below, exactly on, and just above**. For a whole-number limit of 40, that's 39, 40 and 41. For money in naira and kobo, it might be 9,999.99, 10,000 and 10,000.01.
Worked example: a fee rule
The rule: "Orders of ₦10,000 or more ship free. Otherwise, delivery is ₦800." The prices are invented. Here's the code:

A typical test, an order of ₦15,000, gives 0, and an order of ₦3,000 gives 800. Both correct. But the edge test, exactly ₦10,000, gives 800, and the rule says it should be free. The code used `>` where the rule meant `>=`. This kind of mistake, being wrong by exactly one step at an edge, is called an **off-by-one error**, and it's one of the most common bugs in all of programming.

Before running anything, write a **test table**: the input, the result you expect from the rule, and then the result you actually get. Writing the expected column first stops you accepting whatever the program happens to produce.

One row disagrees, and it points straight at the bug. Fixing it is a one-character change, `>` to `>=`, but only the edge test could have found it. Keep the test table after the fix, and run every row again: a change that fixes one row can break another.
Testing only typical values like 3,000 and 15,000. Both pass, and the bug at exactly 10,000 survives. Typical tests show the idea works. Edge tests show the details are right.
A rule usually assumes sensible input, but programs receive whatever they're given. Ask what happens with:

items: **Impossible values**: a mark of 105, or a negative order.
**Zero**: an order of ₦0, or a count of 0.
**Empty text**: nothing typed at all.

blocks.text: Decide on purpose what the program should do, and check for it first:

Checking for invalid input first, before the normal rule, is called a **guard**. It keeps impossible values from quietly getting a normal-looking answer, such as a mark of 105 being reported as a pass.
Edges in security

Attackers test edges on purpose: the 4th login attempt when the limit is 3, a negative quantity in a shopping cart, an empty password. A login that allows "3 attempts" but checks `attempts > 3` before locking actually allows a 4th. The same test table finds it.

warmup.answer: The first branch, because 70 >= 70 is True.

warmup.question: Why is `x == 1 or 2` always True?
warmup.answer: Because the 2 on its own counts as True.

blocks.text: Test a real-style rule and fix it: "Late submissions lose 10 marks if they're up to 3 days late, and get 0 if they're more than 3 days late. On-time work keeps its mark."

items: In the box, the code has a bug at an edge. Before running anything, write a test table for `days_late` = 0, 1, 3, 4 and 10, with the expected final mark for a mark of 70.
Run the code with each value by changing `days_late`, and fill in the actual column.
Find the row that disagrees, and fix the comparison.
Add a guard: a negative `days_late` should set `final` to `"Invalid"`.
**Test my code** checks only the current value of `days_late`. Change it to 0, 1, 3, 4 and −1 in turn, and record each run. Marks here run from 10 to 100, so the 10-mark penalty never goes below 0.

I found the edge where the code was wrong, and fixed the comparison.

exercises.answer: `age < 18`. Test 17, 18 and 19.

exercises.question: Why put the invalid-input check first in a chain?
exercises.answer: So impossible values are caught before the normal rule gives them an ordinary-looking answer.

summary: Every comparison has an edge where its answer flips.
Test just below, exactly on, and just above each edge.
An off-by-one error is being wrong by one step at an edge, often `>` instead of `>=`.
Write expected results before running, in a test table.
Guard against impossible input first, before the normal rule.

lessons.title: Nested decisions (practice)
lessons.goal: Put one decision inside another when a rule needs it, flatten nesting with `and` when it doesn't, and practise writing and testing full decision rules from start to finish.
lessons.why: Some rules have layers: first you check one thing, and only then does a second question make sense. Nesting decisions handles these. But deep nesting makes code hard to read and easy to get wrong, so knowing when to flatten it matters as much. This practice lesson also brings together everything in this unit: comparisons, chains, combined conditions, edges and guards.

blocks.text: A **nested decision** is an `if` inside another `if`'s block. The inner question is only asked when the outer one was True.
Indentation shows the layers. The inner `if` and `else` are indented once more than the outer `if`, so they belong inside it. The outer `else` lines up with the outer `if`.
Nesting fits when the inner question only makes sense after the outer one. Asking about a mark only makes sense for a registered student, so the mark check sits inside.

Trace it as Python does. The outer condition, `registered`, is True, so Python enters the outer block and meets the inner `if`. The mark, 55, is at least 40, so it prints "Passed" and skips the inner `else`. Since the outer condition was True, the outer `else` is skipped too. If `registered` had been False, Python would have jumped straight to the outer `else`, without ever looking at the mark.
Nesting is often used when it isn't needed. These two versions do the same thing:

blocks.code:
if age >= 18 and has_id:
    print("Allowed")

blocks.text: The flat one is shorter and easier to read. Use `and` when both conditions simply need to be True together, and there's nothing different to do when only one of them is.

head: Use nesting when
Flatten with and when
rows: Each layer has its own else
Both conditions just need to be True
The inner check only makes sense after the outer one
Neither condition depends on the other

blocks.text: Nesting four or five levels deep. Each level adds indentation and makes it harder to see which else belongs to which if. If you're nesting deeply, try a flat elif chain with guards first.

sections.title: Turning a layered rule into code

blocks.text: Use the same steps as before, with one more question: does this check depend on another?
Worked example: a hostel allocation rule
The rule: "Only registered students can apply. Final-year students get priority. Others get a room if their fees are paid, and go on the waiting list if not." This is an invented example.

This rule could have been nested, but a flat chain with a guard first is easier to read. The guard, `if not registered`, handles the case where nothing else matters. Then the remaining checks run in order of priority.
Test it like any decision

Notice how the guard row says "anything" for the other two facts. Once a student isn't registered, nothing else changes the answer, so one test covers all four of those combinations. That's another benefit of putting guards first: they make the test table smaller.

Every row of the rule needs at least one test. With three true or false facts, there are eight combinations in total. You don't always need all eight, but you need one for each different outcome, and any combination you're unsure about.
For each rule in today's practice:

items: Write the outcomes.
Decide which checks depend on others.
Write a guard for impossible input.
Write the chain, flat where you can.
Write a test table with expected results before running.

Nest when each layer has its own else, or the inner check depends on the outer.

lessons.title: Repeat work with loops
lessons.goal: Repeat steps with a `while` loop, make sure every loop moves towards its end, trace a loop by hand, and stop a loop early with `break`.
lessons.why: Repetition is the third structure, and it's what makes computers worth using. A person gets bored adding a hundred numbers. A computer adds a million without complaint, as long as you tell it exactly when to keep going and when to stop. Loops are behind nearly every useful program: processing every student in a register, every line of a log file, every row of a dataset.

blocks.text: A `while` loop repeats its block for as long as its condition stays True. Python checks the condition, runs the block if it's True, then goes back and checks again.

blocks.code:
count = 1
while count <= 3:
    print("Round", count)
    count = count + 1
print("Finished")

blocks.text: Like `if`, the `while` line ends with a colon, and the block is indented. Each run through the block is called an **iteration**. When the condition becomes False, Python skips the block and carries on with the next unindented line.
A loop that works has three parts, and forgetting any one causes a bug.

head: Part
In the example
What goes wrong without it
rows: NameError, or the loop starts in the wrong place
It runs the wrong number of times

blocks.text: Tracing a loop
Trace a loop exactly as you trace any code: one row each time the condition is checked.
The condition is checked **four** times for **three** iterations. The last check is the one that's False and ends the loop.
If the condition never becomes False, the loop runs forever. That's an **infinite loop**.

This forgets the update, so `count` stays 1, and `1 <= 3` is always True. The program prints "Round 1" forever. In a lesson box, it would eventually be stopped. In a real program, you'd need to force it to stop, usually with Ctrl and C.

Updating the wrong variable, or in the wrong direction. Starting with a positive balance, `while balance > 0:` with `balance = balance + 100` inside never ends, because the balance only grows. Ask: does every iteration move closer to making the condition False?

sections.title: Loops that run until something happens

blocks.text: A `while` loop is the natural choice when you don't know in advance how many times to repeat: you keep going until something happens.
Worked example: saving towards a target
You have ₦2,000 and save ₦1,500 a week. How many weeks until you have ₦10,000? The amounts are invented.

blocks.code:
savings = 2000
weeks = 0
while savings < 10000:
    savings = savings + 1500
    weeks = weeks + 1
print(f"{weeks} weeks, with ₦{savings:,}")

blocks.text: You didn't need to work out the number of weeks beforehand. The loop found it by repeating until the target was reached. This is something a single calculation can't easily do when the rule each week is more complicated, such as interest or a fee that changes.
`break` ends a loop straight away, even if its condition is still True. It's useful when you find what you were looking for partway through.
The loop would normally run until `n` reached 100, but as soon as it finds 56, `break` stops it.
while True

Sometimes the clearest loop is one that runs "forever" and stops with `break` when something happens. This pattern, `while True:` with a `break` inside, is common for menus and for asking until a valid answer is given. Make sure the `break` can really be reached, or it's an infinite loop.

warmup.question: What does `x = x + 1` do?
warmup.answer: Takes the current x, adds 1, and stores the result back in x.

warmup.question: Why does a loop need to change something?
warmup.answer: If the condition starts True and nothing changes it, the loop never ends.
