lessons.title: For loops and ranges
lessons.source: The Python Tutorial · for statements and range
lessons.goal: Repeat something a set number of times with `for` and `range`, go through every character of a string or every item in a group, and choose between `for` and `while`.
lessons.why: Most loops in real programs go through a known set of things: every student, every day of the week, every line of a file. A `for` loop does that directly, with no counter to set up or update, so there's less to get wrong. `range` is the standard way to count, and its one surprise, that it stops before its end number, causes some of the most common bugs in Python.

blocks.text: A `for` loop takes each item from a group, one at a time, and runs its block once for each.

blocks.code:
for course in ["COS 102", "STA 111", "CSC 183"]:
    print("Registered:", course)
blocks.output:
Registered: COS 102
Registered: STA 111
Registered: CSC 183

blocks.text: The values in square brackets are a **list**, a group of values in order. You'll learn lists properly in the Collections unit. For now, it's enough to know that a `for` loop can go through them.

Each time round, the **loop variable**, here `course`, holds the next item. You choose its name. The loop ends by itself when there are no items left. There's no start, condition or update to write, which is why `for` loops are less likely to go wrong than `while` loops.
`range` gives a sequence of integers. It's the usual way to repeat something a set number of times.

blocks.code:
for week in range(1, 4):
    print("Week", week)

blocks.text: `range(5)` gives five numbers, from 0 to 4. That's convenient for counting how many times, but it means that to get 1 to 10, you write `range(1, 11)`.
Writing `range(1, 10)` and expecting 10 to be included. It stops at 9. The end number is always left out. This off-by-one error is one of the most common in Python.
Repeating a set number of times
When you don't need the number itself, only the repeats, the loop variable can be named `_`, which tells readers "this isn't used":

blocks.code:
for _ in range(3):
    print("Practice!")

blocks.text: A string is a sequence of characters, so a `for` loop can go through it one character at a time:
This combines a loop with a decision inside it, which is how most real loops work. The loop goes through every item, and the decision picks out the ones that matter.

Trace the start of it. `vowels` starts at 0. The first letter is "P", which isn't in "aeiou", so nothing happens. Then "r", also not a vowel. Then "o", which is, so `vowels` becomes 1. The loop carries on through every letter, and only the three vowels, o, a and i, add to the count. Capital letters wouldn't count with this check, since "A" isn't in "aeiou". To count those too, you could loop through `"Programming".lower()` instead.
Both repeat, but they suit different situations.

head: Use for when
Use while when
rows: You go through a known group of items
You repeat a set number of times
You don't know how many times in advance
Every student, every day, every character
Until the target is reached, or until a valid answer

blocks.text: Any `for` loop over a range can be written as a `while` loop, but the `for` version is shorter and safer:

head: `for`
Equivalent `while`
rows: `i = 0`, then `while i < 3:` with `i = i + 1` at the end of the block

blocks.text: The `while` version has three parts to get right. The `for` version has none. When a `for` loop fits, use it. Save `while` for the loops where you genuinely can't know the number of repeats before you start.

warmup.answer: A start, a condition, and an update that moves towards the end.

warmup.answer: Being wrong by exactly one step at an edge.

lessons.title: Loop patterns
lessons.goal: Recognise and write the five loop patterns that most programs use: totals, counts, the largest or smallest, searching, and checking whether every item passes.
lessons.why: Most loops you'll ever write follow a handful of patterns. Once you can recognise them, a new problem stops being a blank page: you ask which pattern fits, and you already know its shape. These patterns are the backbone of data processing in statistics, of log analysis in security, and of everyday programs that summarise lists of anything.

blocks.text: An **accumulator** is a variable that collects a result as the loop goes. It starts at a neutral value, and each iteration adds to it.

blocks.code:
marks = [65, 72, 58, 80]
total = 0
for mark in marks:
    total = total + mark
print("Total:", total)
print("Average:", total / len(marks))

blocks.text: The shape is always the same: **start before the loop, update inside it, use it after it**. Here, `len(marks)` gives how many marks there are, just as `len` gave the length of a string.
`total = total + mark` can also be written `total += mark`. The two mean exactly the same.
Setting the accumulator inside the loop. If `total = 0` is indented inside the `for`, it resets on every iteration, and you're left with only the last mark.
A **counter** is an accumulator that adds 1 each time an item matches a condition.
To find the largest value, keep the largest seen so far, and replace it whenever you find a larger one.

`marks[0]` means the first item in the list. Start with an actual item, not 0. If you start at 0 and every value is negative, such as temperatures below freezing, the answer would wrongly be 0. Python also has built-in `max` and `min` that do this for you, but knowing the pattern lets you find the largest by any rule you need, such as the longest name.
To find whether any item matches, loop until you find one, then stop with `break`.

blocks.code:
courses = ["COS 102", "STA 111", "CSC 183"]
wanted = "STA 111"
found = False
for course in courses:
    if course == wanted:
        found = True
        break
print("Found" if found else "Not found")

blocks.text: `found` is a **flag**: a bool that starts False and becomes True when something happens. `break` stops the loop as soon as the answer is known, since there's no point checking the rest.
The last line uses a short form of if and else, written on one line: `"Found" if found else "Not found"` gives one value or the other.

sections.title: Checking all: does every item pass?

blocks.text: The opposite question is whether **every** item passes. Start by assuming yes, and look for one that fails.

blocks.code:
marks = [65, 72, 58, 80]
all_passed = True
for mark in marks:
    if mark < 50:
        all_passed = False
        break
print(all_passed)

blocks.text: One failure is enough to make the answer False, so the loop can stop there. Only when the loop finishes without finding a failure is the answer True.

Search and check-all are mirror images. Search asks "is there at least one?" and starts by assuming no. Check-all asks "are they all?" and starts by assuming yes. In each case, a single item can settle the answer, which is why both can use `break`. You can often combine several patterns in one loop, as long as each has its own variable, set up before the loop starts.

head: Pattern
Starts at
Inside the loop
Question it answers
rows: Set True and break when found
Set False and break when one fails

lessons.title: Nested loops
lessons.goal: Put one loop inside another to work through grids and pairs, work out how many times the inner block runs, and recognise when nested loops get slow.
lessons.why: Many problems have two dimensions: rows and columns in a table, every day of every week, every pair of students. One loop handles one dimension. A loop inside a loop handles two. Nested loops are also where programs first become slow, because the work multiplies, and recognising that early is the start of thinking about efficiency, which matters later in algorithms and data analysis.

blocks.text: A **nested loop** is a loop inside another loop's block. For each single iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs all the way through.

blocks.output:
Week 1, Mon
Week 1, Tue
Week 1, Wed
Week 2, Mon
Week 2, Tue
Week 2, Wed

blocks.text: The outer loop picks week 1, then the inner loop goes through all three days. Only then does the outer loop move on to week 2, and the inner loop goes through all three days again. It's like the hands of a clock: the minute hand goes all the way round for each single step of the hour hand.

Indentation shows which loop each line belongs to. The inner `for` is indented once, inside the outer loop. The `print` is indented twice, inside the inner loop, so it runs for every combination of week and day. Tracing a nested loop works the same way as any loop, with a column for each loop variable: the inner variable changes on every row, and the outer one only changes when the inner loop starts again.
The inner block runs **outer count × inner count** times. Above, that's 2 × 3 = 6.

That last row is why nested loops matter for speed. A single loop over 1,000 items does 1,000 steps. A loop over 1,000 items inside another loop over 1,000 does a million. For large data, a nested loop can turn a program that takes a second into one that takes a long time. You'll study this properly in the algorithms course, but it's worth noticing from the start.
A nested loop is the natural way to go through anything with rows and columns. Here's a multiplication table:

`{row * col:4}` makes each number 4 characters wide, so the columns line up. Notice where things go: `line = ""` is inside the outer loop, so each row starts fresh, and `print(line)` is after the inner loop, so a row is printed once it's complete.

Putting a line at the wrong level of indentation. If `print(line)` were inside the inner loop, it would print a growing row after every single number. Ask of every line: should this run once per row, or once per cell?

To look at every pair of items, such as every match between teams, loop over the items twice. To avoid pairing an item with itself, and to avoid counting each pair twice, start the inner loop just after the outer one:

`range(len(teams))` gives positions 0 to 3. For position 0 the inner loop runs for 1, 2 and 3. For position 1, it runs for 2 and 3. And so on. Four teams give 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 pairs. In maths, this is the number of ways to choose 2 from 4.
Breaking out of nested loops

`break` only stops the loop it's directly inside. In a nested loop, it ends the inner loop, and the outer loop carries on. To stop everything, set a flag in the inner loop, and check it in the outer one.

lessons.title: Tracing loops by hand (practice)
lessons.goal: Trace any loop by hand with a table, predict its exact output before running it, and answer exam questions that ask what a loop prints.
lessons.why: "What does this code print?" is one of the most common exam questions in first-year programming, nearly everywhere, and it's done on paper. It's also the skill that lets you read code someone else wrote, and find the line where your own code goes wrong. Loops are where tracing matters most, because the same lines run many times with different values.

blocks.text: A trace table has a column for each variable that changes, and a column for the condition or the loop variable. Add one row each time a variable changes, or each time the loop goes round. Add an output column for anything printed.
Worked example: a while loop

blocks.code:
n = 1
total = 0
while n <= 4:
    total += n * n
    n += 1
print(total)

blocks.text: The rules that make it reliable:

items: **Write the starting values first**, before the loop.
**Do the lines in order**, exactly as written, even when you think you know the pattern.
**Use the new value** of a variable as soon as it changes. In step 1, `total` uses `n = 1`, and only then does `n` become 2.
**Check the condition** at the top of every round, including the last one that's False.

blocks.text: Look closely at the last row of the worked example. After the fourth round, `n` becomes 5, and Python goes back to the top to check the condition once more. `5 <= 4` is False, so the loop ends, and only then does the `print` after the loop run. That final check is easy to forget, and forgetting it is how people end up one round out.
Guessing the pattern after two rows and skipping ahead. Loops often change behaviour near the end, at a boundary. Trace every row, at least until you've practised enough to be sure.
For a `for` loop, the loop variable takes each value in turn, so it gets its own column.
For a nested loop, give each loop variable a column. The inner variable changes on every row. The outer one changes only when the inner loop starts again.

Read the table row by row. When `i` is 1, `range(1)` gives just 0, so the inner loop runs once and prints `1 0`. Then the outer loop moves on, `i` becomes 2, and the inner loop starts again from the beginning, this time with `range(2)`, giving 0 and then 1.
Notice that the inner loop's range depends on `i`, so it runs once when `i` is 1, and twice when `i` is 2. Questions like this test whether you really follow the inner loop starting again each time.
When a question asks what code prints:

items: **Find every variable**, and make a column for each, plus Output.
**Write the starting values**.
**Trace line by line**. Write each printed value in the Output column as it happens.
**Check the edges**: the first iteration, the last, and the moment the loop ends.
**Write the final output exactly**, on separate lines if there were separate prints.

blocks.text: Most marks are lost by stopping one iteration too early or too late, and by printing inside the loop when the print is really after it. Watch the indentation of every `print`.

Tracing gets faster with practice. At first, write every row in full. As you become confident, you'll be able to track simple loops in your head and only write rows for the tricky parts, such as the first round, the last round and the exit. But in an exam, a neat table is worth the extra minute: it's easier to check, and it shows the examiner your reasoning.

lessons.title: Finding and fixing loop bugs (practice)
lessons.goal: Recognise the common loop bugs on sight, find them with traces and well-placed prints, fix them, and test the fix at the edges.
lessons.why: Loops go wrong in a small number of ways, again and again: one round too many or too few, never stopping, resetting a total by accident, or a line at the wrong indentation. Knowing these by name means that when your loop gives a wrong answer, you have a short list to check instead of staring at the code. This practice lesson is debugging, which is how most programming time is really spent.

Symptom
Typical cause
rows: One item too many or too few
No update, or the update goes the wrong way
Prints too often, or only once
A line inside the loop that should be after it, or the reverse
A condition that's False from the start

blocks.text: When a loop gives a wrong answer, go down this list. Most bugs are one of these.

Each bug has a recognisable symptom, so start from what you can see. Too many or too few items points to off by one. A program that never finishes points to an infinite loop. A total that equals the last item points to a reset inside the loop. Output repeated many times points to indentation. Matching the symptom to the bug narrows your search from the whole program to one or two lines, which is the difference between debugging for a minute and debugging for an hour.
Off by one

blocks.code:
total = 0
for day in range(1, 7):
    total += 1
print(total, "days")

blocks.text: Meant to count 7 days of a week, it counts 6, because `range(1, 7)` stops at 6. The fix is `range(1, 8)`, or `range(7)` if the day numbers themselves don't matter.
Reset inside the loop

blocks.code:
for mark in [60, 70, 80]:
    total = 0
    total += mark
print(total)

blocks.text: The total should be 210. Because `total = 0` is inside the loop, it resets every round, leaving only the last mark. Move it above the loop.
Wrong indentation

blocks.code:
count = 0
for word in ["a", "bb", "ccc"]:
    count += 1
    print("Words so far:", count)
blocks.output:
Words so far: 1
Words so far: 2
Words so far: 3

blocks.text: If only the final count was wanted, the `print` belongs after the loop, with no indentation. Indentation decides whether a line runs once per round or once in total.
Loop never runs

blocks.code:
n = 10
while n < 5:
    n += 1
print(n)

blocks.text: The condition is already False the first time, so the block never runs. That might be correct, or it might be a reversed comparison. Check what was intended.

sections.title: Finding a bug you can't see

blocks.text: When reading isn't enough, make the loop show you what it's doing. Add a `print` inside the loop that shows the loop variable and the key values each round:

blocks.code:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 4):
    total += i * 2
    print("i =", i, "total =", total)
blocks.output:
i = 1 total = 2
i = 2 total = 6
i = 3 total = 12

blocks.text: This is a trace table that the computer writes for you. Compare it with the trace you expected, and the first line that disagrees shows the round where it goes wrong. Remove these debugging prints once the bug is fixed.
After a fix, don't stop at "it works now". Test the cases that loops get wrong:

items: **An empty input**: a list with nothing in it. Does it crash, or give a sensible answer?
**One item**: does a single round work?
**The boundary**: the first and last values, such as day 1 and day 7.
**A typical input**, to be sure the main case still works.

blocks.text: Fixing a bug by adding or subtracting 1 until the answer looks right, without understanding why. You may fix one case and break another. Find the cause, fix that, then test the edges.

warmup.question: What's an off-by-one error?
warmup.answer: Being wrong by one step at an edge, such as `range(1, 10)` when 10 was meant to be included.

warmup.question: What does an infinite loop forget?
warmup.answer: An update that moves the condition towards False.

summary: Loop bugs are usually off by one, infinite, reset inside, wrong indentation, wrong start, or never running.
Go down the list when a loop gives a wrong answer.
A print of the key values each round is a trace the computer writes for you.
Find the cause, don't just add or subtract 1.
After a fix, test empty, one item, the boundaries and a typical case.

lessons.title: What a function is
lessons.goal: Say what a function is, use Python's built-in functions, define your own with `def`, and call it as many times as you need.
lessons.why: As programs grow, the same steps appear in many places. A function packages those steps under a name, so you write them once and use them anywhere. That makes programs shorter, easier to read, and easier to fix: a bug in a function is fixed in one place, and every use benefits. Functions are how every large program is organised, and you've already been using them: `print`, `len` and `round` are all functions.

blocks.text: A **function** is a named piece of code that does a job. You **call** it by writing its name followed by brackets, with any values it needs inside them.

These are **built-in functions**, which come with Python. You don't need to know how `len` counts the characters. You only need to know what to give it and what it gives back. That's the power of a function: it hides the details behind a name.
You make a function with `def`, short for define. Give it a name, brackets and a colon, then indent the steps that belong to it.

blocks.code:
def greet():
    print("Welcome to 4YOS")
    print("Let's study.")

greet()
greet()
blocks.output:
Welcome to 4YOS
Let's study.
Welcome to 4YOS
Let's study.

blocks.text: The `def` block on its own does nothing visible. It only **defines** the function, telling Python what `greet` means. The steps run when the function is **called**, with `greet()`. Here it's called twice, so the steps run twice.
Forgetting the brackets. `greet` on its own just refers to the function and does nothing. `greet()` with brackets calls it.
Order matters

A function must be defined before the line that calls it. Python reads from the top, so a call above the `def` causes a NameError, because Python hasn't met the name yet. That's why programs usually put all their `def` blocks first, and the code that uses them after.
When Python reaches `greet()`:

items: It **jumps** to the first line inside the `def` block.
It **runs** the indented steps, in order.
When it reaches the end of the block, it **jumps back** to just after the call, and carries on.

blocks.text: This jump and return is what lets one block of code be used from many places. Trace it like any other code, keeping a note of where you jumped from, so you know where to return.

In the `greet` example, Python first reads the `def` block and remembers it, without running it. Then it reaches the first `greet()`, jumps into the block, prints the two lines, and comes back. It reaches the second `greet()`, and does exactly the same again. Finally, there are no more lines, so the program ends. Four lines are printed, from a function that contains only two `print` lines, because it ran twice.

A function can be called from inside another function, and that one can call another. Python keeps track of each place it has to return to, in order, so however deep the calls go, each one comes back to exactly where it was called from.

head: Reason
What it means
rows: Write the steps once, call them many times
`print_report()` says what it does better than ten lines of code
A bug fixed in the function is fixed everywhere it's used
You can check each function on its own
Each function solves one small part

blocks.text: A good function does **one clear job**, and its name says what that job is, usually starting with a verb: `print_receipt`, `count_passes`, `check_password`.
A function can contain anything: decisions, loops, even calls to other functions.
`print_week` calls `print_line` twice. Changing the line's style, say from `-` to `=`, needs one change, inside `print_line`, and both lines update.

summary: A function is a named piece of code that does a job.
Call a function with its name and brackets: `greet()`.
`def name():` defines a function. Its steps run only when it's called.
During a call, Python jumps to the function, runs it, then jumps back.
A good function does one clear job, and its name says what.

lessons.title: Parameters and return values
lessons.goal: Give a function the values it needs through parameters, get a result back with `return`, know the difference between returning and printing, and give parameters sensible defaults.
lessons.why: A function that always does exactly the same thing is limited. Parameters let one function work on any values: one `average` function for any set of marks, one `fee` function for any order. Return values let a function hand its result back to the code that called it, so results can be stored, compared and passed on. This is what turns functions from shortcuts into the building blocks of real programs.

blocks.text: A **parameter** is a name in the brackets of a `def`. It's a variable that receives a value each time the function is called. The value you pass in the call is called an **argument**.

blocks.code:
def greet(name):
    print(f"Welcome, {name}")

greet("Ada")
greet("Tunde")

blocks.text: `name` is the parameter. `"Ada"` and `"Tunde"` are the arguments. Each call puts its argument into `name`, then runs the steps. One function now greets anyone.
A function can have several parameters, separated by commas. Arguments are matched to parameters **in order**: the first argument goes into the first parameter, and so on.

Passing arguments in the wrong order. `show_mark(72, "Ada")` prints `72: Ada`. Python can't tell that you meant otherwise. You can make calls clearer by naming the arguments: `show_mark(name="Ada", mark=72)`.
`return` ends the function and hands a value back to wherever it was called. That value can be stored, printed, or used in an expression, just like the result of `len` or `round`.

blocks.code:
def average(a, b, c):
    return (a + b + c) / 3

mine = average(60, 75, 90)
print(mine)
print(average(50, 50, 80) > 55)

blocks.text: Trace the call `average(60, 75, 90)`. Python puts 60 into `a`, 75 into `b` and 90 into `c`. It works out `(60 + 75 + 90) / 3`, which is 75.0, and `return` hands that back. The whole call, `average(60, 75, 90)`, is replaced by its result, 75.0, which is then stored in `mine`. That's why a returned value can go anywhere a value can go: into a variable, into a comparison, or into another function's brackets.
When Python reaches `return`, the function stops at once, even if there are more lines below it. That's useful in decisions:
As before, these grade bands are only an example.

This is the most important distinction in this unit, and the most common confusion. `print` shows a value on the screen, for a person to read. `return` gives a value back to the program, for the code to use. A function that prints a result can't have that result stored or used in a calculation.

blocks.code:
def add_print(a, b):
    print(a + b)

def add_return(a, b):
    return a + b

x = add_print(2, 3)
y = add_return(2, 3)
print("x is", x)
print("y is", y)

blocks.text: `add_print` showed 5 on the screen, but gave nothing back, so `x` holds **None**, Python's special value meaning "nothing". `add_return` gave 5 back, so `y` holds 5.

head: `print` inside a function
`return` from a function
rows: The person looking at the screen
The code that called the function
Can it be stored in a variable?
Can it be used in a calculation?

blocks.text: As a rule, functions that work out a value should **return** it, and let the calling code decide whether to print it. That makes them reusable, and testable. A function that returns a grade can be used in a report, a chart, or a decision. A function that prints a grade can only ever show it on the screen, once.
A parameter can have a **default**: a value used when the call doesn't give one.
The fee and threshold are invented. Defaults let a function handle the usual case simply, while still allowing a different value when needed. Parameters with defaults go after the ones without.

warmup.question: What does `def` do?
warmup.answer: Defines a function. Its steps run only when it's called.

warmup.question: Where does Python continue when a function finishes?
warmup.answer: Just after the line that called it.

summary: A parameter is a name in the def. An argument is the value passed in the call.
Arguments match parameters in order, unless you name them.
`return` hands a value back and ends the function straight away.
Printing shows a value to a person. Returning gives it to the code. A function with no return gives `None`.
Defaults give a parameter a value when the call leaves it out.

lessons.title: Scope
lessons.goal: Say where a variable can be used, know why a function's variables are private to it, and pass data in and out of functions through parameters and return values instead of sharing variables.
lessons.why: Once a program has several functions, the same name might be used in many places. Scope is the set of rules that decides which variable a name refers to at each point. Without these rules, a variable called `total` in one function could quietly overwrite one in another. Understanding scope explains confusing NameErrors, and it's the reason well-written functions only communicate through their parameters and return values.

blocks.text: A variable created inside a function is **local** to it. It exists only while the function runs, and only code inside that function can see it.

blocks.code:
def work_out():
    result = 6 * 7
    return result

answer = work_out()
print(answer)

blocks.text: `result` is local to `work_out`. Once the function returns, `result` is gone. Trying to use it outside causes an error:

blocks.code:
def work_out():
    result = 6 * 7
    return result

work_out()
print(result)
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 6, in <module>
NameError: name 'result' is not defined

blocks.text: The value 42 was returned, but nobody stored it, and the name `result` only existed inside the function. To use a function's result outside, you must **return** it and **store** it, as in the first example.
Parameters are local too. In `def greet(name):`, the parameter `name` exists only inside `greet`.

Think of each call to a function as getting its own fresh, private workspace. Its parameters and the variables it creates live in that workspace. When the function returns, the workspace is cleared away, and only the returned value survives. The next call gets a new, empty workspace, so nothing is left over from the last time. This is why a local accumulator starts fresh on every call, and why one call can't accidentally see another's values.

sections.title: The same name in two places

blocks.text: Because local variables are private, two functions can use the same name without affecting each other.

blocks.code:
def weekly(daily):
    total = daily * 7
    return total

def monthly(daily):
    total = daily * 30
    return total

print(weekly(100), monthly(100))

blocks.text: Each function has its own `total`. Neither knows about the other's. This is exactly what you want: you can write each function without worrying about names used elsewhere.
A variable created outside any function, at the top level of the program, is **global**. Functions can read a global variable:

blocks.code:
pass_mark = 40

def passed(mark):
    return mark >= pass_mark

print(passed(55), passed(30))

blocks.text: But if a function **assigns** to a name, Python treats that name as local to the function, even if a global has the same name. The global isn't changed:

blocks.code:
count = 0

def add_one():
    count = 1
    return count

add_one()
print(count)

blocks.text: Inside `add_one`, `count = 1` creates a new local `count`. The global `count` is untouched, so it's still 0.

Expecting a function to change a global variable by assigning to it. It creates a local one instead. Python does have a `global` keyword that allows it, but changing globals from inside functions makes programs hard to follow, so avoid it.

sections.title: Pass data in, return data out

blocks.text: The clean way for functions to work together is through parameters and return values. Data goes **in** through parameters, and comes **out** through `return`. The function doesn't reach out to change variables elsewhere.

head: Instead of
Do this
rows: A function that changes a global total
A function that takes the old total and returns the new one
A function that reads a global setting
A function that takes the setting as a parameter, perhaps with a default

blocks.code:
def add_cost(total, cost):
    return total + cost

total = 0
total = add_cost(total, 1500)
total = add_cost(total, 800)
print(total)

blocks.text: Each call takes the current total in and gives a new total back, and the calling code stores it. Everything that affects the function is visible in its call, which makes it easy to read, test and reuse. A function like this, whose result depends only on its parameters, is predictable: the same arguments always give the same result.

warmup.question: What's the difference between print and return?
warmup.answer: Print shows a value to a person. Return gives it to the code.

warmup.question: What does NameError usually mean?
warmup.answer: A misspelled name, or a name used before it was given a value.

Parameters are local too.

lessons.title: Breaking a problem into functions
lessons.goal: Take a problem too big to write in one go, split it into small functions that each do one job, decide what each one takes in and gives back, and join them into a working program.
lessons.why: Real programs are far too big to hold in your head at once. The way every programmer copes is **decomposition**: breaking a big problem into small ones, solving each as a function, and joining them. It's also what exam questions mean when they ask you to "design a solution". Once you can do this, the size of a problem stops being frightening, because you only ever write one small piece at a time.

blocks.text: **Decomposition** means splitting a problem into smaller problems, and those into smaller ones again, until each piece is simple enough to write as one short function.
Take this task: "Read a student's marks, work out the average and the grade, and print a short report." It feels like one job, but it's really several:

head: Piece
What it does
Takes in
Gives back
rows: Turns a score into a grade
Puts it all together and prints
A name and a list of marks

blocks.text: Each piece is small, has one clear job, and can be written and checked on its own. The grade bands used below are an example, not any school's real rule.
A reliable way to decompose is **top-down design**:

items: **Write the whole task in one sentence.**
**List the steps** it needs, in plain words.
**Turn each step into a function name**, and decide what it takes in and gives back.
**Write the top function first**, calling the smaller ones as if they already existed.
**Write each smaller function**, and test it on its own.

blocks.text: Step 4 sounds odd, but it works. Writing the top function first shows you exactly what each smaller function must do, before you've spent time on any of them.
Worked example: a marks report

blocks.output:
Ada: average 72.3, grade A
Tunde: average 48.3, grade below C

blocks.text: `sum` is a built-in function that adds up a list, just like the accumulator pattern does by hand. `report` reads almost like the sentence it came from: work out the average, then print it with its grade. All the detail lives in the smaller functions.
A good function does **one** job. A useful test: can you describe what it does in one short sentence, without the word "and"?

head: Function
One job?
rows: `grade(score)`: turns a score into a letter
`process(marks)`: works out the average and prints a report and saves it to a file

blocks.text: A function that does several jobs is harder to test, harder to reuse, and harder to fix. If one part needs changing, you risk breaking the others. Split it.

Writing one huge function, or no functions at all, because the program "works". It may work today, but the first time it needs changing, or the first time something goes wrong, you'll have to understand everything at once. Small functions let you understand one piece at a time.
A very useful split is between functions that **work something out** and functions that **show** it. In the example, `average` and `grade` work things out and return results. Only `report` prints.

That split means the working-out functions can be reused anywhere: in a report, in a chart, in a decision about who needs extra help. If `grade` printed the letter instead of returning it, none of that would be possible.
A main function
Larger programs often put their top-level steps in a function called `main`, and call it once at the end:

blocks.code:
def main():
    report("Ada", [72, 65, 80])
    report("Tunde", [45, 52, 48])

main()

blocks.text: This keeps the program's starting point in one obvious place, and keeps every variable inside a function, local, rather than global.

warmup.question: What should a function do with a result it works out: print it or return it?
warmup.answer: Return it, so the calling code can store, test and reuse it.

warmup.question: What's the clean way for functions to share data?
warmup.answer: Parameters going in, return values coming out.

blocks.text: Decompose and build a small real tool: a weekly budget summary.

Write `days_over(costs, limit)`, returning how many days were over the limit.
Write `summary(costs, limit)`, returning a string like `"Total ₦9,500, 2 days over ₦2,000"`, using the other two functions.
Print the summary for your own limit. Predict it first, then press **Test my code**.

blocks.text: Write each function's job in one sentence, without the word "and".

rubric: Each function does one job, which I can describe without the word "and".
`summary` builds on the other two instead of repeating their work.
My code passes the test, including the empty list and the exact-limit cases.
practice.starter:
spending = [1500, 2500, 800, 3000, 1200, 0, 500]

def total(costs):
    # Replace this line
    return 0

def days_over(costs, limit):
    # Replace this line
    return 0

def summary(costs, limit):
    # Replace this line: use total and days_over
    return ""

assert total([1500, 2500, 800]) == 4800, "total([1500, 2500, 800]) should be 4800"
assert total([]) == 0, "total([]) should be 0"
assert days_over([1500, 2500, 3000], 2000) == 2, "days_over([1500, 2500, 3000], 2000) should be 2"
assert days_over([2000], 2000) == 0, "a day exactly at the limit isn't over it"
assert summary([1500, 2500, 800, 3000, 1200, 0, 500], 2000) == "Total ₦9,500, 2 days over ₦2,000", "check the summary's wording and numbers"

exercises.question: Split "work out a week's spending, find the biggest day, and print both" into functions.
exercises.answer: For example: `total(costs)` returns the sum, `biggest(costs)` returns the largest, and `show(costs)` prints both using the other two.

exercises.question: A function `check_and_save(password)` checks a password's strength and saves it to a file. What's wrong?
exercises.answer: It does two jobs. Split it into `is_strong(password)`, returning True or False, and a separate function that saves.

exercises.question: Why write the top function first, calling functions that don't exist yet?
exercises.answer: It shows exactly what each smaller function must take in and give back, before you write them.

summary: Decomposition splits a big problem into small functions.
Top-down: one sentence, list the steps, name the functions, write the top one first.
A good function does one job, describable without "and".
Keep working out separate from showing: return results, and print in one place.
A `main` function holds the program's top-level steps.

lessons.title: Testing a function
lessons.source: The Python Tutorial · Errors and exceptions
lessons.goal: Check that a function really works by writing tests in code with `assert`, choosing typical, edge and unusual cases, and running them every time the function changes.
lessons.why: A function that looks right isn't the same as a function that is right. Testing by hand, once, catches some mistakes, but a change next week can quietly break it again. Tests written in code can be run in a second, every time anything changes, so mistakes are caught the moment they appear. This is how professional software is kept working, and it's exactly what the **Test my code** button in these lessons has been doing for you all along.

blocks.text: See how the equality case catches an off-by-one condition. Then try the parcel-weight rule yourself.
`assert` checks that something is True. If it is, nothing happens and the program carries on. If it's False, the program stops with an **AssertionError**, showing the message you wrote.

blocks.code:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

assert double(4) == 8, "double(4) should be 8"
assert double(0) == 0, "double(0) should be 0"
print("All tests passed")

blocks.text: Each `assert` line is one **test**: call the function with chosen values, and compare the result with what you know it should be. The message after the comma explains what went wrong if the test fails.
Here's what a failing test looks like:

blocks.code: assert double(4) == 9, "double(4) should be 9"
AssertionError: double(4) should be 9

blocks.text: Here the test itself was wrong: 9 is the wrong expectation. Tests can have mistakes too, which is one reason to work out each expected value carefully, by hand, before you write it down.
The tests you choose matter more than how many you write. For each function, aim for:

head: Kind of test
Why
For `grade(score)`
rows: What should happen with bad input?

blocks.text: The edge tests are the ones that catch off-by-one errors. A grade function written with `score > 70` instead of `score >= 70` passes every typical test and fails only on exactly 70.
Worked example: testing a fee function
The rule: orders of ₦10,000 or more ship free, and others pay ₦800. The amounts are invented.

blocks.code:
def delivery_fee(order):
    if order >= 10000:
        return 0
    return 800

assert delivery_fee(15000) == 0, "a large order ships free"
assert delivery_fee(3000) == 800, "a small order pays 800"
assert delivery_fee(10000) == 0, "exactly 10,000 ships free"
assert delivery_fee(9999) == 800, "just under 10,000 pays 800"
assert delivery_fee(0) == 800, "an empty order still pays"
print("All delivery tests passed")

blocks.text: Five tests, each with a reason. If anyone later changes `>=` to `>`, the third test fails at once and says exactly which case broke.
Testing only the case you were thinking about while writing the function. That's the case most likely to work. Write the edge and unusual tests too, because those are the ones you didn't think about.

In a decomposed program, test each small function on its own before testing the whole. If `average` and `grade` each pass their tests, and `report` still goes wrong, you know the problem is in `report`, the only untested piece.

This is another reason to keep working-out separate from printing. A function that returns a value is easy to test with `assert`. A function that only prints is much harder, because there's no result to compare.
A useful habit is to write the tests **before** the function:

items: Write a few `assert` lines describing what the function should do, including the edges.
Run them. They fail, because the function isn't written yet.
Write the function until every test passes.
Keep the tests, and run them again after every change.

blocks.text: Writing tests first forces you to decide exactly what the function should do, edges and all, before you start. It turns a vague rule into a precise one. Larger courses later call this **test-driven development**.
What tests can't do

Tests show that a function works for the cases you tested. They can't prove it works for every possible input. That's why choosing good cases matters, and why the edges and unusual inputs are worth the extra lines.

warmup.question: Which three values test the edge of `mark >= 40`?
Why should a function that works out a value return it?
warmup.answer: So the calling code can store, test and reuse it.

blocks.text: Write the tests first, then the function.
The rule: `ticket_price(age)` returns 0 for children under 5, 500 for ages 5 to 17, 1000 for ages 18 to 64, and 600 for 65 and over. The prices are invented.

items: In the box, write at least eight `assert` tests: typical ages and every edge (4, 5, 17, 18, 64, 65).
Run them, and see them fail.
Write `ticket_price` until every test passes.
Press **Test my code**, which runs its own tests too.

blocks.text: Write down which edge your first version got wrong, if any.

rubric: I wrote my tests before the function, with every edge included.
Each test checks a returned value with a clear expected result.
My code passes my tests and the lesson's tests.
practice.starter:
def ticket_price(age):
    # Write this after your tests
    return 0

# Write your assert tests here, at least eight, including every edge

print("All my tests passed")

exercises.question: Write two tests for `def square(n): return n * n`.
exercises.answer: For example: `assert square(3) == 9` and `assert square(-4) == 16`.

exercises.question: What happens when an assert's condition is False?
exercises.answer: The program stops with an AssertionError, showing the message.

exercises.question: Which test would catch `score > 70` written instead of `score >= 70`?
exercises.answer: A score of exactly 70.

summary: `assert condition, "message"` does nothing if True, and stops with an AssertionError if False.
Each test calls a function with chosen values and compares the result.
Choose typical, edge, unusual and invalid cases. Edges catch off-by-one errors.
Test small functions on their own first. Returned values are easy to test.
Writing tests first makes the rule precise. Tests can't prove a function works for every input.

further.title: The Python Tutorial, errors and exceptions

lessons.title: Lists
lessons.goal: Store many values in one list, reach any item by its position, change items, add and remove them, and avoid the error that comes from reaching past the end.
lessons.why: Until now, each variable held one value. Real data comes in groups: all the marks in a course, all the fares in a week, every line of a log. A **list** holds a whole group under one name, in order, and lets a loop go through it. Lists are the most used collection in Python, and almost every program you write from now on will use them.

blocks.text: A list is written as values inside square brackets, separated by commas. It can hold any kind of value, and the order is kept exactly as written.

blocks.code:
marks = [65, 72, 58, 80]
courses = ["COS 102", "STA 111", "MTH 101"]
empty = []
print(marks)
print(len(courses))

blocks.text: `len` works on lists just as it does on strings: it gives the number of items. An empty list, `[]`, has length 0. You can mix types in one list, but in practice a list usually holds one kind of thing, such as all marks, or all names, which keeps it easy to work with.
Each item in a list has a position, called its **index**. Python counts positions from **0**, not 1. So the first item is at index 0, the second at index 1, and the last at index `len - 1`.
You get an item by writing the list's name, then its index in square brackets:

blocks.code:
marks = [65, 72, 58, 80]
print(marks[0])
print(marks[2])
print(marks[-1])

blocks.text: Negative indexes count from the end: `-1` is the last item, `-2` the one before it. That's handy when you want the last item and don't want to work out the length first.

Counting from 0 feels strange at first. One way to think of it: the index is how many steps you take from the start. The first item is zero steps from the start, so its index is 0. This is the same reason `range(4)` gives 0, 1, 2, 3: those are exactly the four indexes of a four-item list.
Asking for an index that doesn't exist causes an **IndexError**:

blocks.code:
marks = [65, 72, 58, 80]
print(marks[4])
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 2, in <module>
IndexError: list index out of range

blocks.text: The list has four items, at indexes 0 to 3. Index 4 would be a fifth item, which doesn't exist. This is the off-by-one error again, now with lists. When you see an IndexError, check whether you've counted from 1 instead of 0, or used `len(list)` as an index instead of `len(list) - 1`.
Writing `marks[len(marks)]` to get the last item. The last index is `len(marks) - 1`, or simply `marks[-1]`.
Unlike strings, lists can be changed after they're made. You can replace an item by assigning to its index:

blocks.code:
marks = [65, 72, 58, 80]
marks[2] = 61
print(marks)

blocks.text: Lists also have methods for adding and removing items:

head: Method
What it does
Example
rows: Puts x at index i, moving the rest along
Removes the first item equal to x
Removes the last item, and gives it back

blocks.code:
fares = []
fares.append(500)
fares.append(1200)
fares.append(700)
fares.remove(1200)
print(fares)

blocks.text: Starting with an empty list and appending as you go is one of the most common patterns in programming. It's how you collect results inside a loop, such as every mark above a pass mark.

Notice a difference from strings here. String methods like `.upper()` give you a **new** string and leave the original alone. List methods like `.append()` **change the list itself**, and give back nothing. So you write `fares.append(500)` on its own line, not `fares = fares.append(500)`. That second version would store `None` in `fares`, losing the whole list.
A for loop goes through a list's items in order, which is how you use every item:
This builds a new list containing only the marks that passed. The pass mark of 50 here is only an example. You'll see more ways of working through lists in the next lesson.

warmup.question: What does `len("Ada")` give?
What does a for loop over `[10, 20, 30]` do?
warmup.answer: Runs its block three times, once for each item.

exercises.answer: `"Tunde"` and `"Ngozi"`.

summary: A list holds many values in order, inside square brackets.
Indexes start at 0. The last item is at `len - 1`, or `-1`.
An index past the end causes an IndexError.
Lists can be changed: assign to an index, or use append, insert, remove and pop.
List methods change the list itself, so don't assign their result back.

lessons.title: Working through lists
lessons.goal: Use Python's built-in tools on lists, take a slice of a list, loop with positions, sort, check whether a value is present, and build new lists from old ones.
lessons.why: Once your data is in a list, most questions about it are the same few: how many, how much in total, which is biggest, is this one there, what are they in order. Python has quick, reliable tools for each. Knowing them lets you answer real questions in one line, while knowing the loop patterns from the Loops unit means you understand what those tools are doing underneath.

blocks.text: Python has functions that do the common loop patterns for you:

blocks.code:
marks = [65, 72, 58, 80]
print(sum(marks) / len(marks))
print(max(marks) - min(marks))

blocks.text: The first line is the average: the total divided by the count. The second is the **range**, the gap between the largest and smallest, a simple measure of spread you'll use in statistics. Each is one line, where a loop would take four or five. Use these functions when they fit. Write the loop yourself when you need something they don't do, such as counting only the marks above a limit, or finding the longest name.
Be careful with an empty list. `sum([])` is 0, which is fine, but `max([])` causes an error, and `sum([]) / len([])` divides by zero. If a list might be empty, check `if marks:` first.
A **slice** takes part of a list. Write the start and stop indexes with a colon between them. As with `range`, the stop is left out.

blocks.code:
weeks = ["w1", "w2", "w3", "w4", "w5", "w6"]
print(weeks[0:3])
print(weeks[2:])
print(weeks[-2:])

blocks.text: Leaving out the start means "from the beginning", and leaving out the stop means "to the end". So `weeks[-2:]` is the last two items. A slice gives a new list, and leaves the original unchanged. Slices work on strings too: `"Programming"[0:3]` is `"Pro"`.
A plain for loop gives you each item, but not its position. When you need both, use `enumerate`, which gives the index and the item together:

`start=1` makes the numbering begin at 1, which suits a list shown to people. Without it, `enumerate` starts at 0, matching the list's indexes. Each time round, the loop puts the position in `number` and the item in `course`.
There are two ways to sort, and the difference matters.

blocks.code:
marks = [65, 72, 58, 80]
top = sorted(marks, reverse=True)
print(top)
print(marks)

blocks.text: `reverse=True` sorts from largest to smallest. `sorted` left `marks` in its original order. Use `sorted` when you still need the original order, and `.sort()` when you don't. Strings sort alphabetically, but capitals come before lower case, so tidy the case first if that matters.
`in` checks whether a value is in a list, giving True or False. It's the search pattern in one word:

blocks.code:
registered = ["COS 102", "STA 111"]
print("STA 111" in registered)
print("PHY 101" not in registered)

blocks.text: `.count(x)` gives how many times x appears, and `.index(x)` gives the position of its first appearance, which causes an error if it isn't there. So check with `in` before using `.index`.

sections.title: Building a new list from an old one

blocks.text: Often you want a new list made from some or all of an old one: the marks that passed, or every price with tax added. The pattern is an empty list and `append` inside a loop:

blocks.code:
prices = [1000, 2500, 400]
with_tax = []
for price in prices:
    with_tax.append(price * 1.075)
print(with_tax)

blocks.text: The 7.5% here is only an example rate. Python also has a short way to write exactly this pattern, called a **list comprehension**: `[price * 1.075 for price in prices]`. It means "make a list of `price * 1.075` for each price in prices". You can add a condition: `[m for m in marks if m >= 50]` keeps only the passing marks. Comprehensions are neat, but the loop version is easier to read when you're starting out, and it does exactly the same thing.
Changing a list while looping over it, such as removing items inside a `for` loop over the same list. Items get skipped, because the positions shift under the loop. Build a new list instead.

warmup.question: What does `[5, 8, 2][0]` give?
How do you find the largest value with a loop?
warmup.answer: Start with the first item, and replace it whenever you find a larger one.

summary: `len`, `sum`, `max`, `min` and `sorted` do the common list jobs in one line.
A slice `x[a:b]` takes items a up to b − 1, as a new list.
`enumerate` gives each item's position along with the item.
`sorted(x)` gives a new list. `x.sort()` changes x and gives None.
`in` checks whether a value is present. Build new lists with append, or a comprehension.

lessons.title: Strings as sequences
lessons.goal: Treat a string as a sequence of characters: reach any character by its index, take slices, split text into a list of words and join words back into text, and know why a string can't be changed in place.
lessons.why: A great deal of real data arrives as text: a line from a file, a name typed into a form, a date like "2026-11-06", a line in a security log. To use it, you need to pull pieces out of it, split it into parts, and put parts back together. Because a string is a sequence, almost everything you learned about lists, indexes, slices, loops and `in`, works on text too.

blocks.text: A string is an ordered sequence of characters, so each character has an index, starting at 0, exactly as in a list.

blocks.code:
code = "STA 111"
print(code[0])
print(code[-1])
print(len(code))

blocks.text: The space counts as a character too, at index 3. Negative indexes count from the end, as with lists, and asking for an index past the end causes an IndexError.
Slicing works on strings exactly as on lists: `text[start:stop]`, with the stop left out.

blocks.code:
date = "2026-11-06"
year = date[0:4]
month = date[5:7]
day = date[8:]
print(year, month, day)

blocks.text: This is a common real task: pulling the parts out of text with a fixed layout. Every date written this way has the year in positions 0 to 3, the month in 5 and 6, and the day in 8 and 9, so the same slices work for any date in that form. The pieces are still strings. Convert them with `int` if you need to do arithmetic, as in `int(month)`.

sections.title: Strings can't be changed in place

blocks.text: Unlike lists, strings are **immutable**: once made, they can't be changed. Assigning to one character fails:

blocks.code:
name = "ada"
name[0] = "A"
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 2, in <module>
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

blocks.text: To "change" a string, you build a new one and store it, for example with a slice and `+`: `name = "A" + name[1:]` gives `"Ada"`. That's also why string methods such as `.upper()` and `.replace()` always return a **new** string rather than changing the old one. Lists, by contrast, are **mutable**, so list methods like `.append()` change the list itself.
Calling a string method and expecting the original to change. `name.upper()` on its own does nothing lasting. Write `name = name.upper()` to keep the result.
`split` breaks a string into a list of pieces. With no argument, it splits on any spaces, and ignores extra ones. With an argument, it splits on that exact text.

blocks.code:
sentence = "learn   python   step by step"
words = sentence.split()
print(words)
print(len(words), "words")

row = "Ada,72,COS 102"
parts = row.split(",")
print(parts)

blocks.text: Splitting on a comma is how you read one line of a CSV file, a format you'll meet in the next unit. Each piece is a string, so `parts[1]` is the text `"72"`, not the number 72.
`join` does the opposite: it glues a list of strings into one string, with the string you call it on placed between each piece.

blocks.code:
words = ["Computer", "with", "Statistics"]
print(" ".join(words))
print("-".join(["2026", "11", "06"]))

blocks.text: The syntax looks backwards at first: the separator comes first, then `.join`, then the list. Read `" ".join(words)` as "join the words with a space between them". Every item in the list must be a string, or join fails.
Strings have methods for finding things inside them:

head: Method
Gives
Example
Result
rows: Index of the first x, or -1

blocks.text: `.find` returns -1, rather than causing an error, when the text isn't there. That makes it safe for checking and then slicing:

blocks.code:
email = "ada@mail.com"
at = email.find("@")
print(email[:at])
print(email[at + 1:])

blocks.text: This splits an email address into the part before the @ and the domain after it, by finding the @ and slicing either side of it.
Looping over characters
A for loop over a string gives one character at a time, which is how you check every character:
`.isdigit()` is True for the characters 0 to 9. Strings also have `.isalpha()` for letters and `.isupper()` for capitals, which are useful when checking passwords or typed codes.

warmup.question: What does `"  ada ".strip()` give?

blocks.text: Pull apart real-looking text records.

Set `name` to the name, `course` to the course code, and `mark` to the mark as an int.

Set `label` to the three parts joined with `" | "`, such as `"Ada | COS 102 | 72"`.
Predict, run, and press **Test my code**. Then try another record in the same layout.

What does `"a,b,,c".split(",")` give?

summary: A string is a sequence: index it from 0, slice it, loop over it.
Strings are immutable. Build a new string and store it to "change" one.
`split` turns text into a list of pieces. `sep.join(list)` glues them back.
`.find` gives an index or -1. `in`, `.count` and `.startswith` search too.
Pieces from split are strings. Convert them before doing arithmetic.

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.goal: Store values under names instead of positions with a dictionary, look values up, add and change them, loop through them, and use a dictionary to count things.
lessons.why: A list finds things by position: the third mark, the last fare. But often you want to find things by name: the mark for COS 102, the phone number for Ada, the price of a data bundle. A **dictionary** stores pairs, a key and its value, so you can look a value up directly by its key. Dictionaries are everywhere in real programs: settings, records, counts, and data read from the web.

blocks.text: A dictionary holds **key: value** pairs inside curly brackets. You look up a value by putting its key in square brackets.
Each key appears only once, and leads to exactly one value. Keys are usually strings or numbers. Values can be anything: numbers, strings, even lists. `len` gives the number of pairs.

Think of a dictionary like a real one: you look up a word, the key, to find its meaning, the value. You don't need to know what page it's on, which is what a list's index would be. You only need the word.

When should you choose a dictionary over a list? Ask how you'll find things. If you'll go through the items in order, or ask for "the third one", a list fits. If you'll ask for something by its name, such as "the mark for STA 111", a dictionary fits, and saves you searching the whole list each time.
Assigning to a key adds it if it's new, or replaces its value if it already exists:

blocks.code:
marks = {"COS 102": 72}
marks["STA 111"] = 65
marks["COS 102"] = 75
print(marks)

blocks.text: The first assignment added a new pair. The second replaced COS 102's value, because that key was already there. To remove a pair, use `del marks["STA 111"]` or `marks.pop("STA 111")`. Dictionaries keep their pairs in the order they were added.

sections.title: Looking up a key that isn't there

blocks.text: Asking for a key that doesn't exist causes a **KeyError**:

blocks.code:
marks = {"COS 102": 72}
print(marks["PHY 101"])
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 2, in <module>
KeyError: 'PHY 101'

blocks.text: There are two safe ways to look up a key that might be missing. Check first with `in`, which tests the keys:
Or use `.get`, which gives a default value instead of an error:
Using `in` on a dictionary and expecting it to check the values. `72 in marks` is False, because `in` looks at the keys only. Use `72 in marks.values()` to search the values.
A for loop over a dictionary gives its keys. To get keys and values together, loop over `.items()`:

head: Method
Gives
rows: Each key and value as a pair

blocks.text: `.values()` works with `sum`, `max` and `min`, so the average here is one line.
The most useful pattern for dictionaries is counting how often each thing appears. Each new thing becomes a key, and its value is its count:

`counts.get(name, 0)` gives the count so far, or 0 if this is the first time the name has appeared. Adding 1 and storing it back updates the count. This one pattern answers a huge range of questions: how many times each word appears in a text, how many failed logins came from each address, how many students took each course. In statistics, it builds a **frequency table**.
A dictionary can also hold a whole record, with each key naming one field:

blocks.code:
student = {"name": "Ada", "level": 100, "courses": ["COS 102", "STA 111"]}
print(student["name"], "takes", len(student["courses"]), "courses")

warmup.question: What does `["a", "b", "c"][1]` give?
What's the counter pattern?
warmup.answer: Start at 0, and add 1 each time an item matches.

summary: A dictionary stores key: value pairs. Look up a value by its key: `d[key]`.
Assigning to a key adds it, or replaces its value.
A missing key causes a KeyError. Check with `in`, or use `.get(key, default)`.
`in` checks keys only. Loop with `.items()` for keys and values together.
Counting: `counts[x] = counts.get(x, 0) + 1`.

lessons.title: Sets
lessons.goal: Use a set to keep only unique values, remove duplicates from a list, check membership quickly, and combine sets with union, intersection and difference.
lessons.why: Many real questions are about which different things there are, not how many times each appears: which courses has any student registered for, which addresses appeared in a log, which words are used in a text. A **set** holds each value once, and answers "is this in it?" very quickly. Sets also bring the union and intersection from the sets you met in maths straight into code.

sections.title: A set holds each value once

blocks.text: A set is written with curly brackets, like a dictionary, but with single values instead of key: value pairs. Any repeated value is kept only once.

"COS 102" was written twice, but the set holds it once, so it has three items. Sets have **no order** and no positions, so you can't index them: `courses[0]` is an error. When printed, their items may appear in any order.
An empty set must be written `set()`. Writing `{}` makes an empty dictionary, not a set.
The most common use of a set is removing duplicates from a list. Convert the list to a set, and back if you need a list again:

blocks.code:
visits = ["10.0.0.5", "10.0.0.9", "10.0.0.5", "10.0.0.5", "10.0.0.2"]
unique = set(visits)
print(len(visits), "visits from", len(unique), "addresses")
print(sorted(unique))

blocks.text: `sorted` turns the set into an ordered list, which is the usual way to show a set's contents tidily. If the original order matters, sets aren't the right tool, since they forget it.
`.add(x)` puts a value into a set. Adding a value that's already there does nothing, with no error. `.discard(x)` removes a value if it's there.

blocks.code:
seen = set()
for word in "the cat and the dog and the bird".split():
    seen.add(word)
print(len(seen), "different words")

blocks.text: Checking `x in some_set` is very fast, even for a set of millions of items, because Python doesn't search through them one by one. Checking `x in some_list` has to look at each item in turn. For a big collection that you check many times, such as a blocklist, a set is much quicker. For a list of ten items, you'll never notice the difference. For a list of a million items checked thousands of times, it can be the difference between an instant answer and a long wait.
These work exactly as in maths, with symbols:

head: Operation
Symbol
Gives
Maths
rows: `a` pipe `b`, written with the vertical bar key
In a but not in b

blocks.text: `required - done` gives the courses still to do. `required & done` gives the ones finished. Questions like "what's left?", "what do these two have in common?" and "what's in either?" become one line each.

The union symbol is the vertical bar, the key usually found above Enter. All three operations give a new set and leave the originals unchanged. They're the same operations you met in Sets and Logic, now on real data. Order matters for difference: `required - done` is the courses still to do, while `done - required` would be any finished courses that weren't required, which is a different question. Union and intersection give the same answer either way round, just as A ∪ B equals B ∪ A in maths.

Using a set when order or repeats matter. A set of exam marks loses repeated marks, so two students with 65 count once, and the average comes out wrong. Use a set for "which different values", and a list for the actual data.
Which collection so far?

warmup.answer: True.

warmup.question: In maths, what's the intersection of two sets?
warmup.answer: The elements that are in both.

exercises.question: How do you remove duplicates from a list `names`?
exercises.answer: `set(names)`, or `sorted(set(names))` for an ordered list.

exercises.question: With `a = {1, 2, 3}` and `b = {2, 3, 4}`, what are `a & b` and `a - b`?

summary: A set holds each value once, with no order and no indexes.
`set(list)` removes duplicates. An empty set is `set()`, not `{}`.
`in` on a set is very fast. `.add` and `.discard` change it.
`|` is union, `&` is intersection, and `-` is difference.
Use a set for unique values, a list for ordered data with repeats.

lessons.title: Tuples
lessons.goal: Group a few related values into a tuple, unpack them into separate names, return several values from one function, and know when a tuple suits better than a list.
lessons.why: Some values belong together and shouldn't change: a date's day, month and year, a point's x and y, a course code and its units. A **tuple** keeps such a group together and protects it from being changed by accident. You've already used tuples without noticing: `for course, mark in marks.items()` hands you a tuple each time round. Tuples also let a function give back more than one result, which you'll use often.

blocks.text: A tuple is written as values separated by commas, usually inside round brackets:

blocks.code:
point = (3, 4)
date = (6, 11, 2026)
course = ("STA 111", 3)
print(date[0], date[2])
print(len(course))

blocks.text: Indexing, slicing, `len` and `in` work on tuples exactly as on lists. The difference is in what you can't do.
A tuple with one item needs a trailing comma: `(5,)`. Without the comma, `(5)` is just the number 5 in brackets, the same brackets you use in arithmetic.
Like strings, tuples are **immutable**. Once made, their items can't be replaced, added or removed:

blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 2, in <module>
TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

blocks.text: That's a feature, not a limitation. When a group of values describes one fixed thing, such as a date or a coordinate, immutability means no part of your program can quietly change one piece and leave the group inconsistent. To "change" a tuple, you build a new one: `date = (date[0], 12, date[2])`.

head: List
Tuple
rows: A few items that belong together

blocks.text: **Unpacking** puts each item of a tuple into its own name, in one line:

blocks.code:
course = ("STA 111", 3)
code, units = course
print(code, "has", units, "units")

blocks.text: The number of names on the left must match the number of items, or Python raises a ValueError. Unpacking is what's happening in `for course, mark in marks.items()`: each pair from `.items()` is unpacked into two names.
Unpacking gives a neat way to swap two variables, with no temporary variable needed:

blocks.code:
a = 5
b = 9
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)

blocks.text: Python first builds the tuple `(b, a)` from the right side, which is `(9, 5)`, then unpacks it into `a` and `b`.
A function can return only one value, but that value can be a tuple. So a function can hand back several results at once, and the caller unpacks them:

`return min(values), max(values)` builds a tuple of two values. The caller unpacks it into two names. This is far cleaner than writing two separate functions that each go through the same list, or storing results in global variables.

You've seen this already with the built-in `divmod`, which returns a whole quotient and a remainder together: `hours, minutes = divmod(135, 60)` gives 2 and 15 in one step, the same as `135 // 60` and `135 % 60`. Whenever a calculation naturally produces two or three linked answers, returning them as a tuple keeps them together, and the caller decides what to call each one.
Unpacking into the wrong number of names. `a, b = (1, 2, 3)` causes a ValueError: too many values to unpack. Count the items, and use the same number of names.
Because tuples can't change, they can be used as dictionary keys, which lists can't. That lets you look things up by a combination of values:

blocks.code:
timetable = {("Mon", 8): "COS 102", ("Mon", 10): "STA 111", ("Tue", 8): "MTH 101"}
print(timetable[("Mon", 10)])

blocks.text: The key `("Mon", 10)` means "Monday at 10". A list such as `["Mon", 10]` can't be a key, because a list could be changed after it was stored, which would break the lookup. Python insists that dictionary keys never change.

warmup.question: Can you change one character of a string in place?
warmup.answer: No. Strings are immutable, so you build a new string.

warmup.question: What does `.items()` give when you loop over a dictionary?
warmup.answer: Each key and value as a pair.

summary: A tuple groups a few related values: `(3, 4)`. One item needs a comma: `(5,)`.
Tuples are immutable, so a fixed group can't be changed by accident.
Unpacking puts each item into its own name: `code, units = course`.
A function can return several values as a tuple, which the caller unpacks.

lessons.title: Choosing a collection
lessons.goal: Choose the right collection for a job by asking how the data will be used, combine collections, such as a list of dictionaries, and work through real-shaped data with loops.
lessons.why: You now know four collections: lists, dictionaries, sets and tuples. Choosing well makes a program short and clear. Choosing badly makes it long, slow or buggy: searching a list when a dictionary would look it up instantly, or using a set and losing repeated values you needed. Real data also comes combined, such as a list of records where each record has named fields, which is exactly the shape of a spreadsheet or a database table.

sections.title: Ask how the data will be used

blocks.text: The right collection depends on what you'll do with the data, not on the data itself. Four questions decide it:

head: Question
If yes
rows: Will I look items up by a name or code?
Do I only care which different values there are, or whether something is present?
Is it a small fixed group that belongs together, such as a date?
Otherwise: items in order, perhaps with repeats?

blocks.text: The same data can call for different collections depending on the question. Take the courses a student has passed:

head: Question about the passed courses
Best collection
rows: Print them in the order they were taken
What mark did I get in STA 111?
Which required courses haven't I passed yet?
Each record of course code and units

blocks.text: The two "instantly" cells matter for large data. Checking `x in a_list` looks through items one by one. Looking up a key in a dictionary, or checking `x in a_set`, goes straight there, however large the collection is.

Real data rarely fits one simple collection. Collections can hold other collections. The most common shape is a **list of dictionaries**: a list of records, each record a dictionary with the same keys. It's exactly how a table with named columns looks in code.

Each item in the list is one row, and each key is one column. Looping over the list gives one record at a time, and `s["mark"]` reads one field. You'll meet this exact shape again when you read CSV files in the next unit, and later when you work with databases and data analysis.
Other useful combinations:

head: Shape
Example
Use
rows: Which courses fall on each day

blocks.text: Worked example: grouping marks by course
A dictionary of lists collects many values under each key. Here's how to build one from a list of records:

The loop unpacks each tuple. The first time a course appears, it gets an empty list. Then each mark is appended to its course's list. This **grouping** pattern, a close cousin of counting, is behind almost every report that summarises data by category.

Searching a long list again and again for one item, such as looping through every student to find one by name each time. If you look things up by name often, build a dictionary keyed by name once, then look up instantly.
Signs that you've chosen the wrong collection:

items: You keep writing loops just to find one item by its name: use a dictionary.
Your totals or averages come out wrong after converting to a set: repeats were lost, so keep a list.
You keep checking whether something is already in a list before adding it: you want a set.
You get a TypeError when using a list as a dictionary key: use a tuple.

blocks.text: Changing collection is usually a small edit, and it often makes the rest of the code shorter.

warmup.question: Which collection removes duplicates?
warmup.answer: A set.

warmup.question: Which collection can be a dictionary key: a list or a tuple?
warmup.answer: A tuple.

exercises.answer: A dictionary, with names as keys and numbers as values.
