summary: Choose a collection by how you'll use the data, not by the data itself.
Look up by name: dictionary. Unique or present: set. Small fixed group: tuple. Otherwise: list.
Dictionary lookups and set membership are instant. Searching a list isn't.
A list of dictionaries is a table: each dictionary a row, each key a column.
Grouping: give each new key an empty list, then append.

lessons.title: Reading files
lessons.goal: Open a text file, read it all at once or line by line, remove the line endings, and turn each line into data your program can use.
lessons.why: Every program so far has lost its data when it finished. Real data lives in files: marks exported from a portal, readings from a sensor, lines in a server log. Reading files lets one program work through thousands of records that nobody would type in by hand. It's also how almost every statistics and security task begins: open the data, and read it.

blocks.text: `open` connects your program to a file and gives you a **file object** to read from. The safest way to use it is inside a `with` block, which closes the file automatically when the block ends, even if something goes wrong part-way.

The lesson boxes in 4YOS have their own small, private file area, separate from your real files. So each example first writes a small file, then reads it. Writing is the next lesson. For now, read the first few lines of each box as "set up a file to read".

blocks.code:
with open("marks.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("72\n65\n80\n")

with open("marks.txt") as f:
    text = f.read()
print(text)

blocks.text: `f.read()` gives the whole file as one string. The `\n` characters are the line endings, which is why each number appears on its own line. The extra blank line at the end comes from the final `\n` plus the line `print` adds.

The filename `"marks.txt"` here is a **relative path**: Python looks for it in the program's current folder. A full path such as `C:/Users/Ada/Documents/marks.txt` names the exact location. Forward slashes work in Python on Windows too, and avoid the trouble backslashes cause inside strings.
For most data, you want one line at a time. Looping over a file object gives each line in turn, including its line ending:

blocks.code:
with open("marks.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("72\n65\n80\n")

total = 0
with open("marks.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        total += int(line.strip())
print("Total:", total)

blocks.text: `line.strip()` removes the `\n` at the end, and any stray spaces. Then `int` converts the text to a number. This loop is the accumulator pattern from the Loops unit, with a file as the source of items instead of a list.
Reading line by line also matters for large files. A log file can be bigger than the computer's memory. Looping reads one line, processes it, and moves on, so it can work through a file of any size.

Forgetting the `
` at the end of each line. `int("72
")` happens to work, because `int` ignores spaces and line endings, but comparing text doesn't: `"Ada
" == "Ada"` is False. Strip each line before using it.
Most data files have one record per line, with fields separated by a character such as a comma. Strip, split, and convert:

blocks.code:
with open("results.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Ada,72\nTunde,58\nNgozi,81\n")

with open("results.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        name, mark = line.strip().split(",")
        mark = int(mark)
        if mark >= 70:
            print(name, mark)

blocks.text: Each line becomes two strings, which are unpacked into `name` and `mark`, and then the mark is converted to a number. The threshold of 70 is just an example.
Blank lines and headers
Real files often have a header line naming the columns, and blank lines at the end. Skip them on purpose:

blocks.code:
with open("results.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("name,mark\nAda,72\n\nTunde,58\n")

with open("results.txt") as f:
    next(f)
    for line in f:
        line = line.strip()
        if not line:
            continue
        print(line.split(","))

blocks.text: `next(f)` reads and throws away one line, the header. `continue` skips straight to the next round of the loop, so the blank line is ignored. The `if not line` check uses truthiness: an empty string is falsy.

head: Code
Gives
rows: The whole file as one string
One line at a time, with its `\n`
A list of every line, each with its `\n`
A list of every line, without line endings

blocks.text: `f.read().splitlines()` is convenient for small files. For large files, prefer the loop.
Text encoding

Text files store characters as bytes, using an **encoding**. The common one today is UTF-8, which can store ₦, accented letters and any language. If a file shows strange characters when read, it may use a different encoding. You can say which with `open("file.txt", encoding="utf-8")`. Writing the encoding explicitly is a good habit, because the default can differ between computers.

warmup.question: What does `"Ada,72".split(",")` give?
What is a file path?
warmup.answer: The location of a file, written as the folders that lead to it, ending in the file's name.

with open("fares.txt") as check:
    rows = [int(x) for x in check.read().splitlines()[1:] if x.strip()]
assert fares == rows, "fares should be every number in the file, in order, as ints"
assert total == sum(rows), "total should be the sum of the fares"
assert count == len(rows), "count should be how many fares there are"
assert average == round(sum(rows) / len(rows), 1), "average should be rounded to 1 place"

exercises.question: Why use `with open(...) as f:` instead of plain `open`?
exercises.answer: The `with` block closes the file automatically when it ends, even after an error.

exercises.question: A line is read as `"Tunde,58\n"`. How do you get the number 58?
exercises.answer: `int(line.strip().split(",")[1])`.

exercises.question: How do you skip a header line before a loop over a file?
exercises.answer: Call `next(f)` once before the loop.

summary: `with open(name) as f:` opens a file, and closes it when the block ends.
`f.read()` gives the whole file. `for line in f:` gives one line at a time.
Each line ends with `\n`. Strip it before comparing or splitting.
Strip, split, convert: that turns each line into data.
Skip headers with `next(f)` and blank lines with `continue`. Say the encoding.

further.title: The Python Tutorial, reading and writing files

lessons.title: Writing files
lessons.source: The Python Tutorial · Reading and writing files
lessons.goal: Save your program's results to a text file, choose between replacing a file and adding to it, and write data in a layout that you or another program can read back later.
lessons.why: A program that only prints loses its results the moment the window closes. Writing to a file keeps them: a report you can hand in, a log of what happened, results another program will read. It's also how programs talk to each other: one writes a file, and another reads it. Writing carelessly can destroy data, though, so knowing exactly what each file mode does matters.

blocks.text: To write, open the file with a **mode**. Mode `"w"` means write: it creates the file if it doesn't exist, and **empties it first** if it does. Then `f.write(text)` adds text.

blocks.code:
with open("report.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Weekly report\n")
    f.write("Total: 4500\n")

with open("report.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())

blocks.text: Two things to notice. `write` doesn't add a line ending, unlike `print`, so you add `\n` yourself. And `write` only takes a string: `f.write(4500)` is a TypeError. Convert numbers first, which an f-string does neatly: `f.write(f"Total: {total}\n")`.

Opening an important file with `"w"` by accident. Mode `"w"` empties the file the moment it opens, before you write anything, and there's no undo. Double-check the mode and filename before running code that writes.
Mode `"a"` means append: it adds to the end of the file, and keeps what's already there. It also creates the file if it doesn't exist.

blocks.code:
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Monday: 2 hours\n")

with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Tuesday: 1 hour\n")

with open("log.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())

blocks.text: Data written to a file isn't always saved to the disk the instant you call `write`. Python collects it and saves it in larger pieces, which is faster. Closing the file makes sure everything is saved, which is one more reason to use `with`: when the block ends, the file is closed, and every line you wrote is really in it.

Choose by what should happen to old contents. A report you rebuild each time suits `"w"`. A log that grows over time suits `"a"`. Mode `"x"` is the safe choice when you must never overwrite something by accident: it refuses if the file already exists.
To save a list of results, loop and write one line each:

blocks.code:
marks = {"COS 102": 72, "STA 111": 65, "MTH 101": 58}
with open("marks.csv", "w") as f:
    f.write("course,mark\n")
    for course, mark in marks.items():
        f.write(f"{course},{mark}\n")

with open("marks.csv") as f:
    print(f.read())

blocks.text: This writes a header line and then one record per line, with a comma between fields. That's a CSV file, the most common format for sharing tables. You'll learn the proper tools for CSV in the next lesson. A file written this way can be opened in a spreadsheet, or read back by your own program with the methods from the last lesson.

`"
".join(lines)` is another way to write many lines at once, when you already have a list of strings: `f.write("
".join(lines) + "
")`.
print to a file
`print` can also write to a file, using its `file` option. It adds the spaces and line ending for you:

blocks.code:
with open("summary.txt", "w") as f:
    print("Total:", 4500, file=f)
    print("Days:", 7, file=f)

with open("summary.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())

sections.title: Write so it can be read back

blocks.text: A file is only useful if it can be read back correctly. Some habits help:

items: **One record per line**, with the same fields in the same order every time.
**A header line** naming the fields.
**A separator that doesn't appear in the data.** A comma is a problem if a field can contain a comma, such as "Port Harcourt, Rivers". The next lesson's `csv` module handles that safely.
**Plain numbers**, without currency signs or thousand separators, so they convert back easily. Format for people only in reports, not in data files.
**UTF-8 encoding**, written explicitly with `encoding="utf-8"`.

blocks.text: The test of a good data file is simple: can your reading code from the last lesson turn it back into exactly the data you started with?

warmup.question: What does a `with open(...) as f:` block do when it ends?
warmup.answer: It closes the file automatically.

warmup.question: What does `f"{2/3:.2f}"` give?

exercises.question: What happens to a file's old contents when you open it with `"w"`?
exercises.answer: They're erased immediately, even before you write anything.

exercises.question: Why does `f.write(42)` fail, and how do you fix it?
exercises.answer: `write` only takes strings. Use `f.write(str(42))` or an f-string.

exercises.question: You add one line per day to a study log. Which mode?
exercises.answer: Append, `"a"`, so earlier days are kept.

summary: Mode `"w"` creates or empties a file, then writes. There's no undo.
Mode `"a"` adds to the end. Mode `"x"` refuses to overwrite.
`write` takes strings only and adds no line ending.
`print(..., file=f)` writes with spaces and a line ending.
Write one record per line, with a header, plain numbers and UTF-8, so it reads back exactly.

lessons.title: CSV data
lessons.goal: Read and write CSV files with Python's `csv` module, get each row as a list or a dictionary, handle fields that contain commas, and convert the text values into numbers.
lessons.why: CSV, short for comma-separated values, is the most common way tables are shared: exports from school portals, data from the National Bureau of Statistics, downloads from a bank, a spreadsheet saved for another program. You've already split lines on commas by hand, which works until a field contains a comma itself. The `csv` module handles every awkward case correctly, and gives you rows in exactly the list-of-dictionaries shape from the Collections unit.

sections.title: What a CSV file looks like

blocks.text: A CSV file is plain text. Each line is one row, and commas separate the fields. The first line is usually a header naming the columns:

blocks.code:
town,state,population
Aba,Abia,534265
"Port Harcourt, city",Rivers,1865000

blocks.text: The second data row has a comma inside its first field, so that field is wrapped in double quotes. The quotes tell a CSV reader "this comma is part of the value, not a separator". Splitting on commas by hand would break this row into four pieces. The `csv` module reads it correctly as three. The population figures here are illustrative only.

`csv.reader` turns each line into a list of strings, dealing with quotes for you. Pass it an open file, and open CSV files with `newline=""`, which the module's documentation recommends so that line endings inside quoted fields are handled correctly.

blocks.code:
import csv

with open("towns.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    f.write('town,state,population\nAba,Abia,534265\n"Port Harcourt, city",Rivers,1865000\n')

with open("towns.csv", newline="") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    header = next(reader)
    for row in reader:
        print(row)
print(header)

blocks.text: `import csv` loads the module, which you'll learn about properly in the Modules lesson. `next(reader)` takes the header row, just as `next(f)` skipped a line in a plain file. Notice that every value is a **string**, including the populations. CSV has no types: it's all text.
`csv.DictReader` uses the header line as keys, and gives each row as a dictionary. This is usually clearer, because you read fields by name instead of by position:

blocks.code:
import csv

with open("towns.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    f.write('town,state,population\nAba,Abia,534265\n"Port Harcourt, city",Rivers,1865000\n')

total = 0
with open("towns.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        total += int(row["population"])
        print(row["town"], "in", row["state"])
print("Total:", total)
blocks.output:
Aba in Abia
Port Harcourt, city in Rivers
Total: 2399265

blocks.text: `row["population"]` is still text, so `int` converts it before adding. Reading by name also means your code keeps working if someone adds a column or changes the column order, which positions can't survive.

Forgetting that CSV values are strings. `row["mark"] > 50` compares text with a number, which is a TypeError. And `"9" > "50"` is True, because text compares character by character. Convert with `int` or `float` before comparing or calculating.
`csv.writer` writes rows from lists, adding quotes wherever a field needs them:

blocks.code:
import csv

rows = [["town", "state"], ["Aba", "Abia"], ["Port Harcourt, city", "Rivers"]]
with open("out.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    csv.writer(f).writerows(rows)

with open("out.csv") as f:
    print(f.read())

blocks.text: The writer added quotes around the field with a comma, and nowhere else. To look at a CSV file you've written, open it normally, without `newline=""`: the csv writer ends each line with the Windows-style ` `, and normal text mode turns that back into ordinary line endings. `writerow` writes one row, and `writerows` writes a list of rows. `csv.DictWriter` does the same from dictionaries, given the list of column names:

blocks.code:
import csv

records = [{"course": "COS 102", "mark": 72}, {"course": "STA 111", "mark": 65}]
with open("marks.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["course", "mark"])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(records)

with open("marks.csv") as f:
    print(f.read())

blocks.text: Real tasks combine everything: read the rows, convert the values, then use the patterns you already know.
Worked example: average mark per course

`setdefault(key, [])` gives the list for that key, creating an empty one the first time. It's a short form of the grouping pattern from the last unit. Read, convert, group, summarise: that sequence is the start of almost every data analysis you'll do in statistics.

warmup.question: What shape is a table in code, with named columns?
warmup.answer: A list of dictionaries: each dictionary a row, each key a column.

warmup.question: What goes wrong if a field such as "Port Harcourt, Rivers" is split on commas?
warmup.answer: The comma inside it splits it into two fields.

exercises.question: Why does `csv.reader` handle `"Port Harcourt, city"` correctly while `split(",")` doesn't?
exercises.answer: The reader understands the quotes, which mark the comma as part of the value.

exercises.question: What type is every value read from a CSV file?
exercises.answer: A string. Convert numbers with int or float.

exercises.question: Why is `DictReader` usually clearer than `reader`?
exercises.answer: You read fields by column name, and the code survives added or reordered columns.

summary: CSV is plain text: one row per line, commas between fields, a header first.
Fields containing commas are quoted. The csv module handles this. Splitting by hand doesn't.
`csv.reader` gives lists. `csv.DictReader` gives dictionaries keyed by the header.
Every value is a string. Convert before comparing or calculating.
`csv.writer` and `csv.DictWriter` write rows, quoting where needed. Open files with `newline=""`.

lessons.title: Handling errors
lessons.source: The Python Tutorial · Errors and exceptions
lessons.goal: Catch errors you expect with `try` and `except`, choose exactly which errors to catch, keep going or report clearly, and raise your own errors when a function gets bad input.
lessons.why: Some errors aren't bugs in your code: they come from the outside world. A person types "twenty" where a number belongs, a file is missing, a value in a CSV is blank. A program that crashes on the first one is fragile. A program that handles them, by asking again, skipping a bad row, or explaining what went wrong, is one people can rely on. Handled carelessly, though, errors get hidden, and hidden errors are worse than crashes.

blocks.text: When Python meets an error while running, it **raises an exception**: it stops what it's doing and looks for code that handles that kind of error. If nothing handles it, the program stops and shows the traceback you learned to read. The error names you've met, ValueError, ZeroDivisionError, KeyError and FileNotFoundError, are all kinds of exception.
`try` marks code that might fail. `except` says what to do if a particular exception happens inside it.

blocks.code:
typed = "twenty"
try:
    age = int(typed)
    print("Next year you'll be", age + 1)
except ValueError:
    print("Please type your age in digits, such as 20.")
print("Carrying on")
blocks.output:
Please type your age in digits, such as 20.
Carrying on

blocks.text: Python runs the `try` block. `int("twenty")` raises a ValueError, so Python stops the `try` block at that line, skips the rest of it, and runs the matching `except` block. Then the program carries on normally after the whole statement. If nothing had gone wrong, the `except` block would have been skipped.
Catching the right error
Name the exception you expect. Each `except` can handle a different one:

blocks.output:
75.0
A mark isn't a whole number.
There are no marks.

blocks.text: Catching everything with a bare `except:` or `except Exception:`. It hides bugs you didn't expect, such as a misspelled variable name, behind your friendly message, so you never find out what really went wrong. Catch only the errors you expect and know how to handle.
Opening a file that isn't there raises a FileNotFoundError. Handling it lets your program explain the problem clearly, instead of showing a traceback:

blocks.output: Couldn't find missing.csv. Check the name and folder.

blocks.text: Skipping bad rows
In real data, one bad row shouldn't stop the whole analysis. Catch the error for that row, count it, and carry on:
Always report how many rows were skipped. Silently dropping data is how wrong results get published.
Two optional parts make the flow clearer:

head: Part
Runs when
rows: Only if a matching error happened

blocks.output:
5 squared is 25
checked 5
x isn't a number
checked x

blocks.text: Keep the `try` block small, holding only the line that might fail. Put what happens next in `else`. That way, an unexpected error in the follow-up code isn't mistaken for the one you meant to catch.
A function can refuse bad input by raising an exception itself, with `raise`:

blocks.output:
25.0
Problem: whole must be more than 0

blocks.text: `except ValueError as error` stores the exception, so you can show its message. Raising an error is better than quietly returning a wrong or made-up value, such as 0, because the caller finds out straight away that something is wrong, and can decide what to do.

warmup.question: What's the difference between a TypeError and a ValueError?
warmup.answer: TypeError: the wrong type. ValueError: the right type, but an unusable value.

warmup.question: What does `int("twenty")` cause?
warmup.answer: A ValueError.

blocks.text: Make a fragile program robust.

items: In the box, `parse_marks(values)` should turn a list of text values into whole-number marks, skipping any that aren't whole numbers, and return a tuple: the list of marks and how many were skipped.
`safe_average(marks)` should return the average, but raise a ValueError with a clear message if the list is empty.
Below them, use both on the real-looking data, catching the ValueError from `safe_average` and printing its message.
Catch only ValueError. Don't use a bare except.
Predict, run, and press **Test my code**.

blocks.text: Write how many values were skipped, and why each one was.

rubric: I caught only ValueError, with small try blocks.
I reported how many values were skipped instead of dropping them silently.
My function raises a clear error for empty input, and my code passes the test.

def parse_marks(values):
    marks = []
    skipped = 0
    # Convert each value, skipping and counting any that fail
    return marks, skipped

def safe_average(marks):
    # Raise ValueError if marks is empty, otherwise return the average
    return 0

data = ["72", "65", "", "80", "n/a", "58"]
marks, skipped = parse_marks(data)
print(marks, skipped)

try:
    safe_average([])
    raise AssertionError("safe_average([]) should raise ValueError")
except ValueError:
    pass

exercises.question: What happens to the rest of a `try` block after the line that raised an error?
exercises.answer: It's skipped. Python jumps to the matching except block.

exercises.question: Why is a bare `except:` a bad idea?
exercises.answer: It hides unexpected bugs behind the same message, so you never find them.

exercises.question: When does a `finally` block run?
exercises.answer: Always, whether or not an error happened.

summary: An exception stops the code and looks for a handler. With none, the program stops.
`try` runs code that might fail. `except SomeError` handles that error only.
Catch specific errors. A bare `except` hides bugs.
`else` runs if nothing failed. `finally` always runs. Keep `try` blocks small.
`raise ValueError("message")` refuses bad input clearly. Report skipped data.

lessons.title: Modules
lessons.goal: Use code from other files with `import`, pick out just what you need, explore what a module offers, and split your own program into modules.
lessons.why: Nobody writes everything from scratch. Python comes with hundreds of ready-made **modules** for maths, random numbers, dates, statistics, files and much more, written and tested by others. Importing them saves you days of work and many bugs. And once your own programs grow, splitting them into modules keeps each file small and focused, which is decomposition at the level of whole files.

blocks.text: A **module** is a file of Python code: functions, values and other tools, under one name. `import` loads a module, and you use its contents with the module's name and a dot:

blocks.code:
import math

print(math.sqrt(49))
print(math.pi)
print(math.ceil(4.2))

blocks.text: `math.sqrt` is the square root function inside the `math` module. `math.pi` is a value stored in it. `math.ceil` rounds up to the next whole number, the opposite of floor division. The dot means "the thing called sqrt that belongs to math". Writing the module's name each time makes it clear where every tool comes from.
Imports go at the top of a file, so a reader sees at once what the program depends on.
There are three common forms:

head: Form
Then you write
Use when
rows: Usually: clearest about where things come from
You use one or two tools from it very often

blocks.code:
from random import choice
import statistics as st

marks = [65, 72, 58, 80, 72]
print(st.mean(marks))
print(st.median(marks))
print(st.mode(marks))

blocks.text: The `statistics` module works out the mean, median and mode for you: the averages you'll study properly in Describing Data. `choice` from the `random` module picks a random item from a list, so its result changes from run to run, which is why it isn't printed here.

Using `from module import *`, which imports everything under its bare name. Names can silently clash: a module's `open` or `sum` could replace the built-in one, and nobody reading the code can tell where a name came from. Import names explicitly.
The modules that come with Python are called the **standard library**. They're always available, including inside 4YOS lessons, with no download.

head: Module
Some of what it does
rows: Square roots, powers, rounding up and down, π
Dates, times and the gaps between them
Reading and writing JSON, a common data format

blocks.text: When you need something common, check the standard library first. Someone has probably solved it already, carefully.
Finding out what a module offers

`dir(module)` lists the names inside a module, and `help(something)` shows its documentation. The online Python documentation describes every module in full, with examples. Reading documentation is a core programming skill: experienced programmers look things up constantly.

blocks.code:
import math

print("sqrt" in dir(math))

blocks.text: Any `.py` file you write is a module, and other files can import it. Suppose a file named `money.py` holds:

blocks.code:
def with_tax(price, rate=7.5):
    return price + price * rate / 100

blocks.text: Then another file in the same folder can write:

blocks.code:
import money
print(money.with_tax(1000))

blocks.text: Splitting a program into files by job, such as one for reading data, one for calculations and one for the report, keeps each file short, and lets you reuse a module in several programs. It's decomposition again, with whole files as the pieces. The 7.5% here is only an example rate. The lesson boxes in 4YOS run one file at a time, so these two snippets are shown as text rather than run.
Code that runs only when the file is run
When a file is imported, all its code runs, including any test prints at the bottom. To keep some code for when the file is run directly, put it under this check:

blocks.code:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(with_tax(1000))

blocks.text: `__name__` is `"__main__"` when the file is run directly, and the module's name when it's imported. So the test print runs when you run `money.py` yourself, and stays quiet when another file imports it.

warmup.question: What does `import csv` let you use?
warmup.answer: The csv module's tools, such as `csv.reader` and `csv.DictReader`.

warmup.question: What's decomposition?
warmup.answer: Splitting a big problem into smaller ones, each solved separately.

blocks.text: Use standard-library modules on real-looking data.

exercises.question: After `import math`, how do you get the square root of 81?
exercises.answer: `math.sqrt(81)`, which gives 9.0.

exercises.question: What's the difference between `import random` and `from random import choice`?
exercises.answer: The first needs `random.choice(...)`. The second lets you write `choice(...)` directly.

exercises.question: Why put test code under `if __name__ == "__main__":`?
exercises.answer: So it runs only when the file is run directly, not when it's imported.

summary: A module is a file of code. `import name` loads it, and `name.tool` uses it.
`from module import tool` and `import module as short` are the other two forms. Avoid `import *`.
The standard library comes with Python: math, random, statistics, datetime, csv, json and more.
`dir` and `help`, and the online documentation, show what a module offers.
Your own `.py` files are modules. Keep test code under `if __name__ == "__main__":`.

lessons.title: Using libraries
lessons.goal: Know the difference between the standard library and packages other people publish, install a package with pip, judge whether a package is safe and worth using, and learn a new library from its documentation.
lessons.why: Beyond the standard library, hundreds of thousands of Python packages solve almost any problem: data analysis, charts, web requests, machine learning. In statistics you'll use pandas and matplotlib. In security you'll use tools built on these packages. Knowing how to find, install and judge a library is as important as knowing the language, and so is knowing the risks, because installing a package means running someone else's code on your computer.

blocks.text: A **package** is a module, or a group of modules, that someone has published for others to use. Most Python packages are published on the **Python Package Index**, called PyPI, at pypi.org. They aren't part of Python, so you install the ones you need.

head: Standard library
Third-party packages
rows: Its own authors, from big teams to one person
No, the boxes run offline with the standard library

blocks.text: **pip** is Python's package installer. On your own computer, in a terminal, not inside Python, you type:

blocks.code: python -m pip install requests

blocks.text: That downloads the package and its dependencies, and installs them, after which `import requests` works in your programs. Writing `python -m pip` instead of plain `pip` makes sure the package goes into the same Python you'll run.

For a real project, programmers usually make a **virtual environment** first: a separate folder of packages for that one project, so two projects needing different versions of a package don't break each other. You'll set one up properly in Programming 2. For now, the idea is enough: each project gets its own packages.
The lesson boxes in 4YOS run Python inside the app, offline, with only the standard library. So this lesson uses standard modules for its runnable examples, and shows pip as text.

sections.title: Judge a package before you install it

blocks.text: Installing a package runs code written by strangers, with the same access to your files as you have. Attackers know this, and publish fake packages with names close to popular ones, such as "reqeusts" instead of "requests", hoping for a typing mistake. This trick is called **typosquatting**. Before installing, check:

head: Check
What to look for
rows: Copy it from the official documentation, don't type it from memory
A known project or organisation, with a link to its source code
Recent releases, and issues that get answered
Widely used in tutorials, courses and well-known projects
That it allows what you plan to do, especially if you'll sell your work
If the standard library does the job, use that instead

blocks.text: Installing a package because a random forum post or video says so, without checking its exact name and source. In security courses you'll see real attacks that started exactly this way.

sections.title: Learning a library from its documentation

blocks.text: Every good library has **documentation**: a guide to what it does and how to use it. A reliable way to learn a new one:

items: **Read the quick-start** or tutorial page first, which shows the most common use.
**Run the smallest example** exactly as written, and check you get the same result.
**Change one thing** at a time, and predict what will happen.
**Look up each function** you use in the reference pages: what it takes, what it returns, and what errors it can raise.

blocks.text: Worked example: learning json from its documentation

The `json` module is in the standard library, so you can try it right here. JSON is a text format for data, used by almost every web service. Its documentation shows two main functions: `json.dumps` turns Python data into JSON text, and `json.loads` turns JSON text back into Python data.

blocks.code:
import json

record = {"name": "Ada", "courses": ["COS 102", "STA 111"], "level": 100}
text = json.dumps(record)
print(text)
back = json.loads(text)
print(back["courses"][1])

blocks.text: Dictionaries, lists, strings and numbers map directly onto JSON, which is why it's so widely used. The documentation also says `json.loads` raises an error if the text isn't valid JSON. That's the step people skip, and it tells you what to catch.
`json.JSONDecodeError` is a kind of ValueError defined in the module. You found it by reading the reference page for `loads`.

warmup.question: What is the standard library?
warmup.answer: The modules that come with Python, always available with no download.

warmup.question: Which import form is usually clearest?
warmup.answer: `import module`, then `module.tool`.

blocks.text: Learn from documentation, and handle data from outside.

items: In the box, `incoming` holds JSON text, such as a web service might send, listing courses and marks.
Parse it with `json.loads` into `data`, catching `json.JSONDecodeError`. If parsing fails, set `data` to an empty dictionary.
Set `best` to the course with the highest mark.
Set `saved` to the data turned back into JSON text with `json.dumps`, sorted by key using the `sort_keys=True` option. You'll find that option in the documentation for `dumps`.
Predict, run, and press **Test my code**. Then break the JSON on purpose, and check your program handles it.

blocks.text: Write what `saved` looked like.

rubric: I parsed the JSON and caught the decode error specifically.
I found an option from the documentation and used it correctly.
My code passes the test, and handles broken JSON without crashing.
practice.starter:
import json

incoming = '{"STA 111": 65, "COS 102": 72, "MTH 101": 58}'

data = {}
best = ""
saved = ""

print(data)
print(best)
print(saved)

lessons.tests:
import json as _j
want = _j.loads(incoming)
assert data == want, "data should be the parsed JSON"
assert best == max(want, key=want.get), "best should be the course with the highest mark"
assert saved == _j.dumps(want, sort_keys=True), "saved should be json.dumps of the data with sort_keys=True"

exercises.question: What is PyPI?
exercises.answer: The Python Package Index, where most third-party Python packages are published.

exercises.question: Why write `python -m pip install` rather than `pip install`?
exercises.answer: It installs into the same Python that you'll run your program with.

exercises.question: What is typosquatting?
exercises.answer: Publishing a harmful package with a name close to a popular one, hoping people mistype it.

summary: The standard library comes with Python. Other packages are published on PyPI and installed with pip.
Use `python -m pip install name` in a terminal, ideally inside a virtual environment.
Installing a package runs strangers' code. Check the exact name, maintainer, activity, use and licence.
Learn a library from its documentation: quick-start, smallest example, change one thing, look up each function.
`json.dumps` and `json.loads` convert between Python data and JSON text.

lessons.title: A small program, start to finish (lab)
lessons.goal: Build a complete small program from a written request: pin down what it must do, design it as functions, write tests first, read real-shaped data, handle bad rows, and produce a report file.
lessons.why: Every lesson so far practised one idea at a time. Real programming asks you to combine them all, starting from a request written in ordinary words, with unclear corners. This lab walks through that whole journey once, carefully, so you know the steps for your course project and for every program after it: understand, design, test, build, check, report.

blocks.text: The request, in ordinary words: "I want to see what I spend on transport each month, by type of transport, and which week was most expensive."
Before writing code, turn it into exact requirements. Ask what goes in, what comes out, and what's unclear.

head: Question
Decision
rows: Where does the data come from?
A summary file: total, total per mode, and the dearest week
Weeks numbered by `date.isocalendar().week`, the international standard
What if a fare is blank or not a number?
Skip the row, count it, and report the count
What if the file is empty?

blocks.text: Writing these down is the most important step. Most failed programs fail here: they solve a slightly different problem from the one that was asked, or they crash on a case nobody decided about.
Split the job so that each function does one thing, and decide what each takes and returns. Keep working-out separate from file handling and printing.

head: Function
Takes
Returns
Job
rows: Valid trips, and the number skipped
A dictionary of mode to total
Group by week, find the largest
Read the file, call the others, write the report

blocks.text: Each trip is a dictionary like `{"date": date(2026, 11, 2), "mode": "bus", "fare": 300}`: the date and fare are converted once, in `parse_rows`, so every later function receives clean data.
Tests describe the decisions from step 1 in code, before any function exists:

blocks.code:
rows = [{"date": "2026-11-02", "mode": "bus", "fare": "300"},
        {"date": "2026-11-03", "mode": "keke", "fare": ""},
        {"date": "2026-11-10", "mode": "bus", "fare": "abc"}]
trips, skipped = parse_rows(rows)
assert len(trips) == 1 and skipped == 2
assert dearest_week([]) is None

blocks.text: Notice what these test: one good row, a blank fare, a non-number fare, and the empty case. These are the decisions most likely to go wrong, which is why they're tested first.

sections.title: Step 4: build, one function at a time

blocks.text: Write the smallest function first, and run its tests before moving on. When `parse_rows` passes, write `totals_by_mode`, and so on. If something fails, you know it's in the function you just wrote.
Worked example: the finished working-out functions

A few new details. `date.fromisoformat("2026-11-02")` turns the text into a real date, and raises a ValueError for a badly written date, so bad dates are skipped like bad fares. `except (ValueError, KeyError)` catches either of two errors: a missing column raises KeyError. `.strip().lower()` tidies the mode, so "Bus" and "bus " count as the same. `max(weeks, key=weeks.get)` finds the key with the largest value, the largest pattern in one line. The 2nd of November 2026 falls in ISO week 45.

When everything passes, go back to the table in step 1 and check each row, one by one. Does the program really answer "which week was most expensive"? Does it handle an empty file? Run it once on a small file whose answers you've worked out by hand. Tests check what you thought of. This final check catches what you forgot.

Stopping when the code runs without errors. Running without errors only proves there are no crashes on that input. Compare the output with answers you worked out by hand, and with the original request.

A short report helps you, a reviewer, or a future employer understand the program: what it does, how to run it, the decisions you made, what it doesn't do, and how you tested it. Your Programming 1 project asks for exactly this.

warmup.question: What are the steps of top-down design?
warmup.answer: One sentence for the task, list the steps, name the functions, write the top one first, then the small ones.

warmup.question: What should happen to bad rows in a data file?
warmup.answer: Skip them, count them, and report the count.

blocks.text: Finish the program by writing the last two functions, then run it from start to finish.

items: In the box, `parse_rows`, `totals_by_mode` and `dearest_week` are written for you. Read them first.

Write `summary_lines(trips, skipped)`, returning a list of lines: `"Total: X"`, then one `"mode: X"` line per mode, sorted by mode name, then `"Dearest week: W (X)"`, or `"Dearest week: none"` if there are no trips, then `"Skipped rows: N"`.
Write `main(in_path, out_path)`, which reads the CSV with `csv.DictReader`, calls the other functions, and writes the lines to `out_path`, one per line.
The box creates `trips.csv` for you. Change it to your own real or likely trips.
Work out the expected report by hand first. Then run it, compare, and press **Test my code**.

blocks.text: Write your hand-worked report, and whether the program matched it.

rubric: I worked out the expected report by hand before running the program.
My functions each do one job, and `main` only reads, calls and writes.
My code passes the test, including the empty case, and handles bad rows by counting them.

lessons.tests:
from datetime import date as _d
t = [{"date": _d(2026, 11, 2), "mode": "bus", "fare": 300}, {"date": _d(2026, 11, 3), "mode": "keke", "fare": 200}, {"date": _d(2026, 11, 10), "mode": "okada", "fare": 600}]
assert summary_lines(t, 1) == ["Total: 1100", "bus: 300", "keke: 200", "okada: 600", "Dearest week: 46 (600)", "Skipped rows: 1"], "summary_lines doesn't match the required layout"
assert summary_lines([], 0) == ["Total: 0", "Dearest week: none", "Skipped rows: 0"], "with no trips, the summary should say Total: 0 and Dearest week: none"
with open("trips.csv", newline="") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
trips, skipped = parse_rows(rows)
with open("summary.txt") as f:
    assert f.read().splitlines() == summary_lines(trips, skipped), "summary.txt should hold the summary lines for trips.csv, one per line"

exercises.question: Why convert dates and fares once, in `parse_rows`?
exercises.answer: So every later function gets clean data, and the conversion and its error handling live in one place.

exercises.question: What does `except (ValueError, KeyError):` catch?
exercises.answer: Either of the two errors: a bad value, or a missing column.

exercises.question: The program runs without errors. Why isn't that enough?
exercises.answer: It only shows there's no crash on that input. The answers must be checked against hand-worked results and the request.

summary: Start by turning the request into exact decisions: inputs, outputs and unclear cases.
Design functions with one job each. Convert data once, at the start.
Write tests first for the risky decisions: bad rows and empty input.
Build one function at a time, testing each before the next.
Check the finished program against hand-worked answers and the original request, then write it up.

further.title: Python for Everybody, the full course

questions.question: What is a program?
answers: A sequence of exact instructions a computer follows literally
questions.feedback: The computer follows each instruction exactly, and fills in nothing.
choices: A machine that solves problems by thinking carefully about each of them, as a person does
A sequence of exact instructions a computer follows literally
A list of rough ideas that the computer completes for you

questions.question: What is the hard part of programming?
answers: Working out exactly what you mean, with every case covered
questions.feedback: Typing is easy. Thinking precisely is the real work.
choices: Typing the code quickly and without spelling mistakes
Working out exactly what you mean, with every case covered
Remembering every single command and symbol in the programming language you use

questions.question: What does the Python interpreter do?
answers: It reads your source code and carries it out, line by line
questions.feedback: The interpreter turns your code into actions.
choices: It reads your source code and carries it out, line by line
It translates English sentences into Python source code
It checks your spelling and grammar carefully before you submit any written work

questions.question: How does a compiled language such as C differ?
answers: It translates the whole program into machine code first, then it runs
questions.feedback: Compilers translate first. Interpreters read and run as they go.
choices: It doesn't need any translation to run on the processor
It translates the whole program into machine code first, then it runs
It can only be used on computers that are connected to the internet

questions.question: What does `print(2 + 3)` show?
questions.feedback: Python works out 2 + 3, then prints the result.

questions.question: Which kind of step is "for every student, print their mark"?
answers: Repetition
questions.feedback: It does the same thing again, once for each student.
questions.part: Programs are made of a few kinds of step
choices: Decision
Repetition
Input

questions.question: A program runs, but gives the wrong total. What kind of bug is it?
answers: Logic error
questions.feedback: It runs, so the syntax is fine, and it didn't crash. The logic is wrong.
choices: Syntax error
Runtime error
Logic error

questions.question: Why are logic errors the most dangerous?
answers: Nothing warns you, and the wrong answer looks confident
questions.feedback: A crash is obvious. A wrong answer can go unnoticed.
choices: Nothing warns you, and the wrong answer looks confident
They always delete files on the computer when they happen
They stop every other program on the computer from running

questions.question: A shop's program charges ₦0 delivery for every order, when only orders over ₦10,000 should be free. What's the most likely cause?
answers: A logic error in how the delivery rule was written
questions.feedback: The program runs, and does exactly what the code says. The rule in the code is wrong.
choices: The computer decided that free delivery would be kinder
A logic error in how the delivery rule was written
A syntax error that stops the program from running at all

questions.question: You're asked to automate a process at work. What should you do before writing any code?
answers: Write down every step exactly, including the unusual cases
questions.feedback: Clear steps first. The code only expresses them.
choices: Write down every step exactly, including the unusual cases
Choose the fastest programming language for the job
Start typing code straight away, then fix what goes wrong

questions.question: A friend says, "The computer got it wrong, even though I told it what I wanted." What's the best reply?
answers: The computer did exactly what the code said, so the fix is in the code
questions.feedback: Computers follow instructions literally. Wrong results come from the instructions.
choices: Computers sometimes choose to ignore what they're told
The computer did exactly what the code said, so the fix is in the code
The computer simply needs more memory installed before it can understand what you want

cards: What is a program?
A sequence of exact instructions that a computer follows literally.
What is source code?
The text of a program, written in a language like Python.
What does an interpreter do?
Reads source code and carries it out, line by line.
What are the three kinds of bug?
Syntax errors, runtime errors and logic errors.
Why test with known answers?
Logic errors give wrong answers without any warning.

questions.question: A procedure says to open the matching file. What rule is still needed if two files have the same name?
answers: Compare their locations and pick the intended folder
questions.feedback: Choosing whichever comes first is a guess, and repeating an identical search changes nothing. The location tells them apart.
choices: Compare their locations and pick the intended folder
Open whichever file happens to appear first in the list
Repeat the same search until only one result remains

questions.question: Which of these is not one of the three basic structures?
answers: Compilation
questions.feedback: The three structures are sequence, selection and repetition.
choices: Selection
Repetition
Compilation

questions.question: `SET total to 0. FOR each number in 3, 4, 5: add number to total.` What's the output of total?
questions.feedback: It goes 3, then 7, then 12.

questions.question: `SET n to 5. WHILE n > 1: SET n to n - 2.` What's n when the loop ends?
questions.feedback: n goes 5, 3, 1. At 1 the condition is false, so the loop stops.

questions.question: `SET n to 5. WHILE n > 0: add 1 to n.` What happens?
answers: It never ends, because n only grows
questions.feedback: The condition stays true forever. A loop has to move toward its end.
choices: It ends when n reaches 0
It never ends, because n only grows
It runs exactly five times

questions.question: A rule applies "for values under 18". Which set best tests the boundary?
questions.feedback: Boundary tests sit on either side of the limit and exactly on it.

questions.question: Why write the expected result before running a test?
answers: So you don't simply accept whatever you get
questions.feedback: Without a prediction, a wrong result can look fine. The prediction is what makes it a test.
choices: It makes the program run noticeably faster when tested
So you don't simply accept whatever you get
Because the computer needs it in order to run the test

questions.question: In a flowchart, which shape normally shows a decision?
answers: A diamond
questions.feedback: Decisions use diamonds with yes and no branches. Rectangles are actions and ovals are start and end.
choices: A rectangle
A diamond
An oval

questions.question: A login allows 3 attempts, then locks the account. A tester tries 3 wrong passwords, and the 4th, correct, password gets in. What kind of error is this most likely?
answers: A boundary error in how the attempts are counted
questions.feedback: The rule breaks exactly at its limit, which is why you test around boundaries. In security, this matters.
choices: A boundary error in how the attempts are counted
A problem with the user's keyboard during the test
A proof that the password is stored too safely

questions.question: You're writing a procedure to find the average of a student's test scores. Which case most needs its own rule?
answers: A student with no tests at all
questions.feedback: With no tests you would divide by zero. Empty input is a classic failure.
choices: A student with four tests
A student with very high scores
A student with no tests at all

questions.question: An online shop gives a discount for orders "over ₦5,000". A customer ordering exactly ₦5,000 complains they got no discount. What should have been done when the rule was written?
answers: Test the exact boundary, and state whether ₦5,000 qualifies
questions.feedback: Words like "over" hide a boundary decision. A boundary test forces you to make that decision on purpose.
choices: Remove discounts from the shop
Test only much larger orders, such as ₦50,000
Test the exact boundary, and state whether ₦5,000 qualifies

cards: What four things does a good algorithm have?
Inputs, outputs, definite steps, and an end.
What are the three basic structures of all algorithms?
Sequence, selection and repetition.
What is a trace table?
A table with a column per changing value and a row per step, for running an algorithm by hand.
What kinds of cases should you test?
Normal, boundary, empty, duplicates or ties, and unexpected input.
Why does a loop need to change something?
Otherwise its condition never changes and it never ends.

questions.question: Which shape shows a decision?
answers: A diamond
questions.feedback: Decisions are diamonds, with Yes and No exits.
choices: A rectangle
A parallelogram
A diamond

questions.question: Which shape shows "INPUT mark"?
answers: A parallelogram
questions.feedback: Input and output use parallelograms.
choices: A parallelogram
A diamond
An oval

questions.question: How many exits does a decision have?
answers: two
questions.feedback: Yes and No, each labelled.

questions.question: Match each shape to its use.
answers: Start or end | A calculation or action | A yes or no question | Input or output
questions.feedback: These four shapes, plus arrows, draw almost any algorithm.

questions.question: What does `IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... END IF` become in a flowchart?
answers: A diamond with two branches that join again below
questions.feedback: The two branches rejoin, so the algorithm carries on.
choices: A single large rectangle that contains both of the choices, written out side by side
A diamond with two branches that join again below
Two completely separate flowcharts, one drawn for each of the choices

questions.question: How is a FOR loop drawn in a flowchart?
answers: As its parts: start a counter, test it, the body, then step it and loop back
questions.feedback: Flowcharts show loops with a decision and an arrow back.
choices: With a special loop-shaped symbol of its own
As its parts: start a counter, test it, the body, then step it and loop back
It can't be drawn in a flowchart at all, so you write it out in words beside the chart

questions.question: Why should the average algorithm check `n = 0` first?
answers: Otherwise it would divide by zero when there are no marks
questions.feedback: Handling the empty case on purpose prevents a crash.
choices: Otherwise it would divide by zero when there are no marks
Because pseudocode always has to start with a decision before any other step can come
Because zero is never a valid number in any algorithm

questions.question: Trace `SET t TO 0. FOR i FROM 1 TO 4: SET t TO t + i.` What is t at the end?
An exam asks for an algorithm that prints whether a number is even or odd. Which pseudocode fits best?
answers: INPUT n. IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN OUTPUT "even" ELSE OUTPUT "odd" END IF
questions.feedback: It's precise: one input, one decision and two outputs. MOD gives the remainder.
choices: Work out if the number is even, and then print the result
INPUT n. IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN OUTPUT "even" ELSE OUTPUT "odd" END IF
Print "even", because most numbers that people use are even

questions.question: A team at work disagrees on how refunds should be handled. How could a flowchart help?
answers: It shows every decision and path, so the team can agree before anyone builds it
questions.feedback: Drawing the decisions makes disagreements visible early.
choices: It shows every decision and path, so the team can agree before anyone builds it
It replaces the need to ever discuss the refund process again
It makes the refund process faster without changing any steps

questions.question: Your flowchart has a branch that never reaches STOP. What does that mean when the algorithm runs?
answers: Following that path, the algorithm never finishes or never gives a result
questions.feedback: Every path must reach an end, or that case is never finished.
choices: Nothing, because the computer will finish that path by itself
Following that path, the algorithm never finishes or never gives a result
The flowchart is fine, as long as most of the paths do reach STOP

cards: What shape is a decision in a flowchart?
A diamond, with two labelled exits.
What shape is input or output?
A parallelogram.
What are the rules for a correct flowchart?
One start, every path reaches an end, decisions have two labelled exits.
How is a loop shown in a flowchart?
An arrow going back up to an earlier step, usually from a decision.
How do you check a design?
Trace it with normal, boundary and empty cases.

questions.question: What does `print("Hello", "Ada")` show?

choices: HelloAda
Hello Ada
"Hello", "Ada"

Predict what the code will print
Add as many lines as you can, to save time

questions.question: You need to work out how many seconds are in a week. Which line does it?

cost_per_day = 800
term_weeks = 13

weekly = days * cost_per_day   # 5 days at ₦800

questions.feedback: One job per function lets each part be built and tested on its own.

Separate functions for each job, joined by a top function

questions.question: A web service sends data as JSON text, and sometimes the text is broken. How should a Python program read it?
answers: Parse it with `json.loads`, catching `json.JSONDecodeError`
questions.feedback: The json module parses the format and reports broken text as a specific error.
choices: Split the text on commas and colons by hand
Parse it with `json.loads`, catching `json.JSONDecodeError`
Assume it's always valid and let any error stop the program
